activity: the idea that historians disagree about the past because sources are partial and questions change
story:
The county archive occupied the second floor of the old library, above the children's room, and Katherine had chosen it because the high school library had nothing on Marco Polo except a picture book with camels on the cover. Her report was due Thursday. She had two days, a partner named Daniel who had not read anything, and a thesis she had written on the bus that morning: Marco Polo's journey opened China to Europe.

The archivist, a small woman named Mrs. Okafor, set her up at a table near the window and brought a slip case of holdings. "Most of what we have is secondary," she said. "Travel narratives, mostly nineteenth century. There's one odd one in there."

Katherine worked through the stack in order. The first books gave her what she expected: seventeen years at the court of Kublai Khan, the Description of the World, the prisons of Genoa where Polo dictated his story to Rustichello. She copied quotations and kept a running page count. By eleven she had half the report drafted in her notebook, and Daniel had texted twice asking if she'd done his half too.

The odd one was a dark blue hardback with a cracked spine, shelved wrong among the admirers. Did Marco Polo Go to China? by Frances Wood. Katherine read the title twice, then the inside flap, then the first chapter standing up because she didn't trust herself to sit still. Wood had argued that Marco Polo might never have reached China at all. Her evidence was the book itself, what it left out. It never mentioned tea. It never mentioned foot-binding. It never mentioned the Great Wall.

She read for an hour without taking a note. When she finally copied the three omissions down, her handwriting came out cramped, as if her hand had a different opinion than her thesis did.

Daniel arrived at noon with a bag of chips and no sources. "Tell me what to say," he said, dropping into the chair across from her. "I'll do the map part. I found a map online."

"Look at this." She turned the blue book toward him and tapped the title.

He glanced at it and pushed the chips aside. "That's dumb. Everyone knows he went. It's like, the most famous trip ever."

"That's the point. She's not saying he lied. She's saying maybe he never reached China, and the book's full of things a person who'd actually lived there would probably mention. Tea, Daniel. Sixteen years in China and no tea."

"So one person says he didn't go. So what? Our report's due Thursday."

Katherine sat back. She wanted to tell him he was missing it, that the report was better now, not ruined, but she could hear how the sentence would sound, like pedantry, like she was grading him instead of persuading him. Mrs. Okafor passed behind them with a cart of document boxes, paused, and said nothing, which somehow felt like permission.

"It's not one person against everyone," Katherine said instead. "It's a question. Historians disagree about him because the sources are partial. We only have his book, and his book doesn't say what we want it to say. Either direction."

"So which side are we on?"

She looked at her notebook, at the thesis she'd written on the bus. Opened China to Europe. It was pithy, it filled a line, and she had believed it that morning without ever having checked whether the journey itself was even settled. She tried to hold both ideas at once, the famous Polo and the doubted one, and found she could do it if she let go of the need for one of them to be wrong. "We're on the question's side," she said. "We present what the book says, then what Wood says, then what we can't know."

"That's not a thesis."

"It is. It's just not the one I started with."

Daniel ate his chips while she drafted. He would still probably only do the map, and she would still probably let him, because she had learned to compartmentalize, to file Daniel under partner in a drawer separate from friend, and to close that drawer when the work mattered. But she drafted differently than she had on the bus. She wrote the admiration first, the courts and the paper money and the years of travel, and then the doubt, set down plainly, without pretending she could settle it: that a traveler who never mentioned the Great Wall had left a crack in his own story, and that historians had been looking through that crack ever since, each one seeing a slightly different China on the other side.

At four Mrs. Okafor came to collect the books. Katherine slid the blue hardback across the table last. "Can I come back tomorrow? I want to reread the chapter on omissions."

"It'll be here," Mrs. Okafor said, and then, almost smiling, "That's the trouble with archives. The books don't change. Only the readers do."

Katherine zipped her notebook into her bag, where it pressed against the folded map Daniel had printed and left behind, the Great Wall drawn across it in a thin red line.

activity: to predict how a change in temperature shifts a reaction at equilibrium using Le Chatelier's principle
story:
The screen door banged behind Nicolas before anyone could tell him not to let it, and he carried his chemistry book and a wrinkled practice sheet out to the kitchen table where his grandfather sat with the newspaper folded to the business section.

"Quiz Friday," Nicolas said, dropping into the chair across from him. "Equilibrium. If I don't pass it, my grade is done for the semester." He smoothed the paper flat against the oilcloth. The problems were about Le Chatelier's principle, predicting which way a reaction would shift when you heated it or cooled it, and the first one wanted him to figure out how many grams of carbon dioxide were involved before he could say anything else.

His grandfather lowered the paper an inch. "When I was your age, we had a teacher who would lambaste you in front of the whole class for forgetting to carry a digit. Called it mathematical illiteracy. I never forgot a digit again."

"I'll try to remember that." Nicolas pulled a pencil from his backpack and wrote the formula at the top of the page. He remembered the atomic masses from the table he'd copied in class: carbon was 12.01, oxygen was 16.00. He added them and wrote the answer in the margin.

His grandmother came through with a dish towel over her shoulder and set a glass of iced tea beside his elbow without asking whether he wanted it. "How is the studying?" she said, and then, to her husband, "Did you take your pills?"

"I took them," his grandfather said, in a tone Nicolas recognized as not entirely reliable. He was eighty-one now, and last month he had told the same story about the 1970s twice in one dinner, first as a story about stagflation and then, forty minutes later, as a story about a man he used to work with, as though the two versions had nothing to do with each other. Nicolas's mother had pulled him aside afterward and said, gently, that it was going to be like this more and more.

Nicolas worked through the calculation. The problem asked how many moles of carbon dioxide were in 88 grams of it, and he divided by what he'd written in the margin and got a little over three, which then fed into the equilibrium question about whether heating the system would push it toward the products or back toward the reactants. He wrote that heating shifted it toward the side that absorbed energy, crossed out the reactants, circled the products, and moved on to the second problem feeling almost steady.

At the second problem, the numbers stopped working. The grams wouldn't divide evenly, the moles came out ugly, and when he tried to fix it by adjusting the equilibrium shift too, the whole answer fell apart. He sat back and stared at the margin where he'd done the simple part, the part that couldn't be wrong. Carbon, 12.01. Oxygen, 16.00. He added them again on a fresh corner of the page and got the same thing he'd gotten before.

Then he looked at his own formula, the CO2 with its small subscript two, and he saw it. Two oxygens. The molar mass of a compound was the sum of the masses of the atoms in its formula, all of them, which meant for carbon dioxide it was 12.01 plus 16.00 plus 16.00 again. 44.01, not 28.01. He had cut the oxygen in half, and everything downstream had been quietly wrong while feeling completely right. He erased the margin, rewrote it, and did the division again with the correct number; the moles came out clean, and the equilibrium answer that had wobbled now sat still.

"I forgot to double the oxygen," he said out loud, half to the table.

His grandfather folded the paper the rest of the way down. His face had that phlegmatic calm it got these days, unhurried, hard to read. "Twice sixteen is thirty-two," he said. "Plus twelve. Forty-four." He tapped the margin with one finger. "My teacher would have loved you today."

"It's not that funny."

"It's a little funny." But he was looking at the page with something more serious underneath, and Nicolas understood, without either of them saying it, that his grandfather had followed the arithmetic perfectly and would maybe not remember, by Sunday, that the conversation had happened at all. Nicolas thought about how the wrong answer had felt just as solid as the right one, and how he would have written it on the quiz with total confidence, and how nothing in the feeling of it would have told him. You just had to go back and count the atoms again, both of them, every time, and even then you couldn't be sure you'd caught everything.

He copied the corrected number onto a clean sheet so it would be the first thing he saw Friday morning. His grandmother took his empty glass and put her hand briefly on his grandfather's shoulder as she passed, and his grandfather covered it with his own hand without looking up from the newspaper.

activity: to direct a one-act play by blocking the actors' movements and running rehearsals
story:
James had won his first two rounds of the tournament, which was, he told himself, exactly according to plan, and so the free hour before round three belonged entirely to the one-act. He had the script in the side pocket of his blazer, three copies, because the cast numbered three, and he had reserved the empty classroom at the end of the humanities hall at eleven, which was a thing he had definitely done rather than a thing he had walked past and found conveniently unlocked.

Priya was already there, sitting on a desk with her heels hooked on the chair rung, and Devon came in late, still carrying his flowpad from the previous round. James arranged the copies on the desk. "We're going to sit and read it first," he said. "No standing, no moving. Just the words."

"A table read," Priya said. "My cousin does community theater. You sit around and read the script through before anybody stages anything, so you can hear how the dialogue actually sounds."

"I was going to say that," James said, and opened his copy, and to be fair to himself he had been going to say something adjacent to it. The classroom smelled of whiteboard marker and the hallway beyond it roared with tab room chaos, forensics kids arguing about speaker points, and here in this pocket of quiet the play began. Priya read the mother. Devon read the son. James read the stage directions in a level voice, unbothered, a director in full command of an incipient production that did not yet exist.

The trouble, in James's private accounting, was small. There was a line on page four where the son tells the mother he never wanted the lake house sold, and when Devon said it aloud it landed with a thud, formal and stagey, nothing like the way any eighteen-year-old on earth would say it to his mother. James had read that line perhaps forty times on his own and it had sounded fine, which was itself informative, since apparently a script sounds one way alone in a bedroom at one in the morning and an entirely different way in a room with other bodies in it. He had believed, before this, that writing was enough, that the page contained the thing. The page did not contain the thing. The thing happened between people, or it did not happen.

"That line's wrong," Devon said, before James could gently arrive at the same conclusion through a series of Socratic questions he had been composing since breakfast. "Nobody talks like that. 'I never consented to the divestment of the property.' Who says that."

"I say that," James said. "In rounds. That's debate. That's the whole problem, actually." And he heard himself say it and understood that it was true, that he had spent four years learning to interpolate evidence into arguments the way a mason slots bricks, and somewhere along the way the mortar had gotten into his ear. He could not tell yet whether the play was an escape from that or just debate wearing civilian clothes. His coach would have said there was a teleology to it, that everything in forensics bends toward the ballot, and James wanted the play to bend toward nothing, but he did not know how to make something bend toward nothing, or even whether that was coherent, whether a story needs a target the way a case needs one.

"We could change it," Priya said.

"I wrote it for the sound of it, not the truth of it," James said. "Or I thought I wrote it for the sound. Let's do the line again." He had them read the scene twice more, seated, scripts flat on the desks, and on the third pass Devon dropped the formal version and said, quietly, "Mom, you sold the lake without asking me," and Priya let the silence run four full seconds before her answer, and the silence did more than either of their lines. James wrote nothing down. He just listened. That was a new instrument and he was not yet sure how to hold it.

Then, because he was who he was, he tried to hold it anyway. He cleared the desks to the wall and stood Devon at the door and Priya at the window, eleven feet apart, which he measured by eye and later described as twelve, and ran the scene again with bodies in it. Blocking, he explained, was the term for where actors move and when, and he had read two chapters about it in a book he would, in later retellings, have studied exhaustively. In fact Devon refused to stand at the door. Devon wanted to sit on the floor with his back against the wall, and James's first instinct was to overrule him, and his second instinct, arriving late but arriving, was to let the actor's body vote. The seated version was worse for the geometry he had imagined and better for everything else.

A girl from another school put her head in the door and said pairing for round three was posting, and Devon left at a run, and Priya folded her copy of the script and put it in her bag and paused at the desk where James was still standing.

"So is the line changing or not?"

"I'll know when I hear it again," James said. "Saturday. My house. Kitchen table, obviously."

"Obviously," Priya said, and knocked twice on the doorframe on her way out, which he chose to take as applause.

activity: to argue both sides of a Supreme Court case about free speech before a mock court
story:
The library's second floor smelled of carpet glue and old bindings, and Laura had claimed the corner table by the window since four o'clock, three legal pads fanned in front of her like cards she was refusing to show anyone. In two weeks she would stand before a panel of local judges at the regional mock court tournament and argue a free speech case, and the tournament's particular cruelty was that each advocate had to argue both sides: petitioners in the morning round, respondents in the afternoon. She had written until the two positions began to bleed into each other, until she could no longer tell which argument she actually believed.

Priya arrived at six with a milkshake and the truculent expression she wore whenever she'd been thinking about something all day and had decided everyone else was behind. "You're doing it wrong," she said, dropping into the chair across from Laura.

"I haven't said anything yet."

"Your face said it. You're trying to pick a side. That's not the assignment. The assignment is to be good enough that the side picks itself for you, both times."

Before Laura could answer, a boy from the study carrels drifted over, backpack straps bunched in one fist. Derek, from her government class, the one who never spoke unless something was actually bothering him. "Can I ask you guys something? You do the mock court thing, right? This morning in first period, Ms. Harrowwell told Marisol she had to stand for the pledge. Not say it, just stand. Marisol said no. She got a referral. So can they make you stand, or not?"

Priya set down her milkshake. "No. West Virginia versus Barnette, 1943. The Supreme Court ruled six to three that public schools cannot force students to salute the flag or recite the Pledge of Allegiance. Marisol should take the referral to the principal and cite it."

Derek repeated the case name back slowly, writing it on his hand. "Nineteen forty-three. Six to three. Okay." He went back toward the carrels, and Laura watched him write it again on a sheet of paper, more carefully, as though his skin might smudge the law.

"That," Priya said, "is your problem in one referral slip."

"What do you mean?"

"You just watched a rule protect somebody. Feels good. Feels like the case is settled, speech wins, done. Then this afternoon you argue the other side, and you'll hate yourself unless you understand why the three dissenters weren't monsters." She tapped Laura's legal pads. "So tell me why a school might want everyone standing. Steelman it. I'll be the judges."

Laura looked at the window, at the parking lot lights coming on. She had been raised in a house where certain words did double duty, where her mother said "community" and meant "obedience," and she'd spent two years at debate learning to call that coercion out loud. Now Priya was asking her to build the case for it. "A school is a small public," she began, halting. "If a public can't ask anything of its members, not even standing, then it isn't a public. It's just a room full of individuals. The three in the majority had utilitarianism on their side and still lost, I mean the dissent, the dissent said the country needed unity more than it needed to protect one conscience."

"Careful," Priya said. "Which three?"

"The three dissenters. In Barnette." Laura heard the words leave her mouth and felt the floor tilt, because she'd had it backward for a week. She'd been telling herself the dissent was about safety in wartime, about order, and that the majority's logic was the utilitarian one, the counting of harms. She grabbed the casebook and turned pages until Justice Jackson's opinion lay open under the desk lamp. She read the line about no official orthodoxy being prescribed by the Supreme Court, then read it again, and something in the argument she'd built for the respondent side, the side defending compelled speech, quietly collapsed and rebuilt itself in a different shape.

"Say what you figured out," Priya said. "Out loud. That's the whole tournament, saying it out loud before a stranger makes you."

Laura closed the book on her thumb. "I had the values reversed. I thought standing together was the practical argument and freedom was the principle. It's not. Compelled unity is the principle, a real one, a whole way of thinking about what a country is, and freedom is the practical one, the thing that actually works, that lets a nation hold people who don't agree. I can argue both now. I understand both now. What I can't do is tell you which one I'd vote for, because I keep switching, and I think switching might be the honest condition."

"That's the answer nobody wants," Priya said, "and the only one worth hearing." She gathered her keys. "Ten tomorrow. Bring the Harwell thing, we can work Marisol into a hypothetical."

Laura stayed after the lights dimmed to the yellow of the night section, copying the case citation onto a fresh card, and she was still there at nine when Derek came back through on his way out. He stopped at her table, and instead of the question she expected, he said, "Marisol stood today. Fourth period, before she even went to the principal. She said the fight was exhausting her more than the pledge did, so she just stood up." He shrugged into his backpack. "Funny, right? You spend all that time learning she doesn't have to, and she goes and does it anyway."

Laura looked down at the card in her hand, Barnette, 1943, six to three, and realized she could not decide whether Marisol had lost something or found it. She slid the card into her pocket next to her speech, where both sides of her argument sat folded together, and started stacking the legal pads to go home.

activity: to compare two apartment leases and work out the total monthly cost including utilities
story:
The laundromat on Felton Street had one working table, and Naomi claimed it at nine forty on a Tuesday night, spreading both leases beside the dryer vents like a general deploying maps. Her mother's clothes tumbled behind her, towels and scrubs and the gray cardigan she wore to every shift, while Naomi smoothed the creased pages and set her phone calculator between them. A boy about her age sat two machines down, watching a sock go around and around as though it owed him money.

"You look like you're planning a war," he said.

"Two apartments. One of them is trying to trick me." She held up the first lease. "This one's twelve hundred a month, but they're giving a month free. The other one's down the street, eleven fifty, no tricks. Or fewer tricks."

He drifted over, dragging his laundry basket with him, and dropped into the chair across from her. His name was Theo, which he offered along with the observation that her spreadsheets were on actual paper, which he called "brave." She called it "my printer is broken," and they agreed to call it brave anyway.

The problem was the free month, which sat in her head like a word she could almost spell. She wrote twelve hundred times twelve on the margin of a flyer for a lost cat named President, then subtracted twelve hundred for the free month, and stared at the number: thirteen-two hundred for the year. She divided by twelve and got eleven hundred even, and sat back so fast the chair squeaked. Eleven hundred. The expensive apartment, with its move-in special, actually came out fifty dollars cheaper every month than the cheap one down the street. She said it out loud to make it real. "One month free on a twelve-month lease at twelve hundred, and it's like paying eleven hundred a month. Not eleven fifty. Eleven hundred."

"Wait, say that again," Theo said, and she did, and he pulled out his own phone to check her arithmetic, which she pretended to resent and secretly appreciated. He was circumspect about it, double-checking her carry on the long division like a man defusing something, but the number held. She wrote EFFECTIVE RENT in block letters, underlined it twice, and felt the particular satisfaction of a trap turned inside out.

Then came the part the flyers had not settled. Utilities. The twelve-hundred building made tenants pay electric and water; the eleven-fifty place covered water but not heat, and heat, in a city whose January she had only visited, was an unknown. She called the electric company's after-hours line and got a recording, called the water department and got a man named Gerald who said, "Can't tell you what your bill'll be, hon, only what mine was," and told her anyway, at length, until she had a number she could predicate nothing on except that Gerald existed and was cold. She laughed, actually laughed, alone in a laundromat at ten twenty, over a stranger's heating bill. Theo laughed too, though he had no idea at whom.

Her mother had texted twice: You decide. Whatever you think. Her mother worked nights and had handed over the leases like a baton, saying only that she'd never been good with this kind of thing, the way people say it about swimming or forgiveness. Naomi understood that whatever she chose, she was choosing for both of them, and that the cheap-looking apartment and the clever-looking apartment and the utilities she could not price until the first true cold snap would all land on the same kitchen table in the spring. The free month was real money, that much she had proven. The rest was weather she hadn't lived through yet.

She folded the leases, one into each back pocket of her jeans, uneven weights, like coins of different countries. The dryer buzzed. She pulled out the gray cardigan and held it a moment, still warm, then folded it over her arm the way her mother liked, sleeves crossed, and texted: The twelve hundred one. I'll tell you why when you're home. Theo raised a hand in salute as she pushed through the door, and outside the night had already gone cold, the wind coming off the parking lot flat and wide as a steppe, and she stood in it a second longer than she needed to, feeling for the first time exactly how much heat costs.

activity: how interest makes borrowed money cost more over time and makes savings grow
story:
The sedan on the showroom floor was silver, or close to it, a shade the brochure called Lunar Mist, and Maria had circled it twice already without touching it, because touching things felt like a first step toward owning them. She had two thousand one hundred dollars in a savings account that her grandmother had started when Maria was nine, an account that had recently begun earning interest, small deposits of money the bank added just for letting it sit there. Forty-one cents last month. Fifty-three the month before. The growth was slow, but it ran in one direction, and she liked that about it.

Her mother was at the sales desk with a man named Duane, who kept sliding papers across the table like a card dealer who already knew the hand. Maria could hear the word "monthly" arriving again and again, a word that sounded small and manageable until you multiplied it by sixty. Sixty months. Five years. The loan on the used sedan, Duane said, could be theirs at seven percent, and he said it the way people say the weather is humid, a condition of the universe rather than a choice anyone had made.

Maria sat down in one of the waiting chairs, which was the exact chair from every dentist's office she had ever visited, and took out her phone. She had gotten her first credit card three weeks ago, a slim blue thing with a limit of five hundred dollars, because the online form had said she was pre-approved and she had wanted, for once, to be approved at something first. She had charged twenty-six dollars at the bookstore. The statement had arrived yesterday with two numbers on it: a minimum payment of twenty-five dollars and a full balance of twenty-six.

She opened the card's app and read the fine print, which was set in gray type on a gray field, evidently designed by someone who hoped she wouldn't. Somewhere in the third paragraph she found the phrase "grace period." It said that a grace period lets you avoid interest on new purchases if you pay the full balance by the due date each month. She read the sentence twice, then a third time, then held the phone away from her face as if distance would make it simpler.

"So if I pay all twenty-six dollars," she said to the empty chair beside her, "they charge me nothing extra."

The empty chair did not adjudicate the matter, but the sentence on the screen seemed to. Pay twenty-six, owe twenty-six. Pay twenty-five, the minimum, and the twenty-six would begin to grow, the way her savings grew but in reverse, in the wrong direction, compounding toward whoever held the debt. It occurred to her that the two systems were mirror images: interest could work for you or against you, and the only difference was which side of the ledger you were standing on. She had always assumed the sides were assigned. Now she suspected they were chosen, or at least drifted into, the way her mother was drifting toward the finance office.

Her mother had been an iconoclast about debt for as long as Maria could remember, the woman who paid cash for a lawnmower, who cut up a store card in the parking lot of the mall while Maria watched through the car window, mortified. And here was that same woman nodding at a payment schedule, because the old car had died on the interstate in February and the new job started Monday and the bus did not run to the office park. Principles, Maria was learning, were not abandoned so much as negotiated with, item by item, in rooms that smelled like new vinyl.

Duane came over with a clipboard and a smile calibrated to the wattage of a man about to save a family. "You're the daughter," he said. "Great. You want to take a look at the payment breakdown? It's a real education."

"I'm already getting one," Maria said, and held up the phone, screen toward him, the grace period sentence still open. She wanted to see whether he would flinch. He did not flinch. He squinted at it with the polite interest of a man being shown a photograph of someone else's children.

"That's a good card," he said. "You pay it off every month, it costs you nothing. More people should start that young." Then, without a seam: "Now, on the sedan, here's what the interest looks like over the life of the loan." He turned the clipboard toward her, and the number at the bottom of the column was larger than the price of the car itself. Not by a little. The car cost eleven thousand dollars, and the loan, over sixty months at seven percent, would cost more than thirteen, and Duane pointed at the monthly figure as though the other number were not also sitting right there, in plain view, waiting to be noticed.

Maria looked from the clipboard to her phone, from the turbid gray paragraph that had quietly told her the truth to the clean white column that was telling her a version of it, and back to her mother, who was signing something at the desk with the pen chained to it. There was a case for the loan; she could make it herself, in her own head, the way a lawyer argues for a client she half doubts. The car meant the job, the job meant the rent, the rent meant they did not move in with Aunt Carol. That was real. But the number at the bottom of the column was also real, and she could not make the two of them agree.

She paid the twenty-six dollars on her phone, the full balance, due date still nine days away, and watched the confirmation appear. Then she walked over to the desk and stood beside her mother, not saying anything yet, just reading the paper upside down, which she had taught herself to do in seventh grade out of boredom and which now, unexpectedly, felt like a kind of power.

"Mom," she said. "Before you sign that last page, can we read the bottom line together?"

activity: to build a portfolio of ten artworks around a single theme with an artist's statement
story:
On the third morning of the portfolio intensive at Camp Wenlock, Morgan spread her nine finished pieces across the floor of the craft lodge and understood, finally, what her advisor had meant when she said a theme had to be a question, not a label. Nine works, and no thread between them except that Morgan had made them: a watercolor of the lake at dawn, a charcoal self-portrait with the eyes left blank, a series of small studies of the dining hall's bent spoons. The tenth was due in two days, along with an artist's statement, and the statement was the part that kept her awake.

"Ten pieces, one idea," said Priya, folding herself down onto the pine boards beside the drawings. Priya was here from a magnet school in the city and kept a sketchbook of hands, only hands, three hundred of them by her own count. "You have nine pieces and zero ideas."

"I have ideas. I just have too many." Morgan straightened the self-portrait so its edge ran parallel with the floorboard. "That's different."

"That's the same thing with better lighting."

The critique session that afternoon made it worse, though not in the way Morgan expected. A boy named Deshawn, presenting his own portfolio, had pinned up a painting of a melted clock over a highway median, and in his statement he'd written that he was working in the tradition of Surrealism. Fine. Then, gesturing at his influences, he said, "Like Frida Kahlo, obviously, the Surrealist," and Priya's hand went up so fast the instructor paused mid-sentence.

"She rejected that label," Priya said. "Breton called her work Surrealist, but she didn't accept it. He said her art was a ribbon around a bomb, and she didn't want the ribbon." Priya was not vitriolic about it; she said it the way she said everything, flat and exact. Deshawn argued that the label fit anyway, that the paintings dreamed, and Priya said that Kahlo insisted she painted her own reality, not her dreams, and that being claimed by a movement you'd refused was its own kind of erasure. The instructor let them go for a full four minutes before moving on, which everyone understood to be a compliment.

Morgan said nothing during the exchange, but afterward, walking the gravel path back to the lodge with her portfolio tube knocking against her knee, she kept turning it over. A ribbon around a bomb. She liked the phrase and distrusted it in equal measure, the way she liked a frame that was prettier than the drawing inside it. Something you wrap around a thing to make it bearable can also be something you use to pretend the thing is a gift. And Kahlo had torn the ribbon off and said, no, this is mine, this is what actually happened to my body, my country, my bed. It was not a dream. It was a Tuesday.

That evening, after lights-out, Morgan sat on the porch of Cabin Four with the camp's one floodlit volleyball court humming yellow in the distance, and she did something she had been avoiding all week: she reread her own statement draft. It was full of ribbons. "Exploring the intersection of memory and place." "Interrogating the ephemeral." Each phrase was a neat bow tied over work that was actually, she could see now, about her grandmother's house being sold in September, about the last summer anyone would sleep in its back bedrooms. She had been wrapping the bomb so skillfully that even she couldn't see it. Her earlier habit of hiding difficult subjects behind pretty language, once a small peccadillo, a charming tic her middle school art teacher had even praised, had quietly become the whole method.

She found Priya at breakfast, carrying her tray of hands to the far table, and sat down across from her without asking. "I need to ask you about the Kahlo thing. Not Kahlo. The principle." Morgan laid out the problem in her plainest voice: nine pieces made out of one real thing, and a statement written to disguise it. "I keep thinking a theme should make the work coherent from the outside. But maybe it's the opposite. Maybe it should hold it together from the inside, where only I can see the join." Priya chewed her toast and said, "Or maybe you pick the theme that scares you, and the coherence is just what's left after you stop arranging." Morgan couldn't tell whether that was wisdom or Priya being Priya, and said so. Priya said, "Both. It's always both," and went back to sketching Morgan's hand where it lay on the table.

Morgan spent the last two days making the tenth piece, which was not, in the end, about the lake or the spoons. She painted the back staircase of her grandmother's house at the moment the movers had carried the mattress down it, the wall scraped pale where the bedframe had caught, and beneath the painting she wrote a single-sentence statement that named the house, the street, the September, and nothing about the ephemeral at all. At final critique, the instructor read it, looked at the staircase for a long moment, and then did something Morgan had not seen her do all session: she picked up the charcoal self-portrait with the blank eyes, the one Morgan had privately considered the weakest piece, and moved it to the center of the lineup.

"That one," she said. "That's where the portfolio starts."

activity: to compare two apartment leases and work out the total monthly cost including utilities
story:
"Your future landlord is not your friend," Ms. Okafor had said on Monday, dropping two photocopied leases on every desk, "and this unit is called Adult Arithmetic, which is a nicer name than the one I wanted to use." Now it was Wednesday, and Anna sat in the back corner of the classroom with both leases side by side, a calculator, and her best friend Devi, who was eating sunflower seeds like a woman watching a disaster unfold at a safe distance.

The problem was straightforward on its face. Lease One, the Marigold Apartments, charged nine hundred a month with the phrase "utilities included" printed in bold at the top, like a trophy. Lease Two, the Halloway Building, charged seven-fifty with "tenant pays all utilities." Anna's worksheet asked for the true monthly cost of each, and at first glance Marigold looked like the obvious winner, a hundred and fifty dollars of free electricity sitting right there.

"Easy," she said, writing 900 in the first blank. "Utilities included means included."

Devi cracked a seed between her teeth. "You know what else means included? Nothing. Words on leases are like my brother's apologies. Technically they exist."

Anna rolled her eyes and started flipping through the photocopied pages anyway, mostly to prove Devi wrong, and that was where the afternoon stopped being easy. On page four of the Marigold lease, in a font size she was fairly sure was illegal, there was a list. Water and trash: included. Heat: included. Electricity: billed to tenant at market rate.

"Wait." She put her finger on the line. "Electricity's not included."

"So it says included but it doesn't mean included."

"It says utilities included and then it picks which utilities." Anna sat back. "So you have to check every single one, separately, or you're just guessing with confidence." She said it out loud mostly for herself, the way she memorized things, and then she recalibrated her whole worksheet in her head: the trophy at the top of the lease was really just a headline, and headlines, as her mother liked to say about the news, were written by people with something to sell.

"Congratulations," Devi said. "You've discovered fine print. Next week: taxes."

"Electricity here runs about eighty a month, the worksheet says." Anna tapped the estimate sheet stapled to the back. "So Marigold is really nine-eighty. And the Halloway, I have to add everything. Water, thirty. Trash, fifteen. Heat, sixty in winter. Electric, eighty."

"It's like stagflation," Devi said solemnly. "Prices up, value down, everyone pretending it's fine."

"That's not what this is."

"It's a vibe, Anna. Let me have it."

Ms. Okafor drifted past their desk, saw the two columns of numbers Anna was building, and said nothing, which in her classroom was the highest form of praise. Anna added the Halloway column twice and got nine-thirty-five both times. So Marigold at nine-eighty, Halloway at nine-thirty-five, a forty-five dollar difference, except the Halloway numbers were estimates, and estimates in winter, according to a warning box on the estimate sheet, could climb like something noxious escaping a lab.

"Forty-five dollars a month isn't nothing," Anna said slowly. "But it's not the hundred and fifty I thought I was saving this morning."

"Or losing. Which one was winning this morning?"

"Marigold. Obviously."

"And now?"

Anna looked at the two leases, at her columns, at the bold word included sitting at the top of one of them like it hadn't just lied to her politely. "Now I don't know. Marigold's cheaper to think about. Halloway's cheaper if the winter's mild, and more expensive if it isn't. The lease doesn't tell you which winter you get."

"That's so cold." Devi pointed at her. "Pun acknowledged."

Anna laughed despite herself, then did the only thing she could honestly do: she wrote both totals on the worksheet, drew an arrow between them, and in the margin added the winter is a variable. It wasn't the answer the blank wanted, probably. The blank wanted a number with a box around it. But she was starting to suspect that adults with boxes around their numbers were exactly the people signing leases like the Marigold, and she had just spent forty minutes learning not to be one of them.

"Time," Ms. Okafor called from the front. "Pencils down. Anna, what did you get?"

Anna held up her worksheet, margin note and all. "Two prices and a weather report."

Devi snorted so hard a sunflower seed shot across the desk and rolled off the edge onto the floor.

activity: to debate whether an ancient religious rule still applies in modern life using the text itself
story:
The horseradish sat on the Seder plate in a small heap, pale and unremarkable, and Priya leaned toward it with the wariness of someone offered a dare. Liam had invited her three weeks ago, after their philosophy club dissolved for the summer on a note of mutual exhaustion, and now she was here at his grandmother's apartment in her one good dress, waiting for someone to explain why everyone was preparing to eat something bitter on purpose.

"That's maror," Liam said. "Bitter herbs. Horseradish, in our family. We eat it to recall the bitterness of slavery in Egypt."

"On purpose," Priya said. "You eat it on purpose."

"Every year."

Across the table, Uncle Martin cleared his throat in the way that meant a performance was beginning. He was the family's raconteur, the man who could turn a two-minute anecdote about a parking ticket into a twelve-minute production with three false endings, and Liam knew the sound of his warming up. "The maror," Martin announced, "is not a symbol, Liam. It is a mandate. That's what your generation misses. The rules were not suggestions."

Liam had spent the drive over rehearsing exactly this argument, because Martin always started it, always before the meal, always with the confidence of a man who had never once lost to a nephew. But this year Liam had done something different. Instead of arguing from the present, from the world he knew, he had spent two evenings with the Haggadah open on his desk, reading the actual text, the way his mother had once suggested and he had never bothered to do.

"The text says we eat it because of the bitterness," Liam said. "It doesn't say it has to be horseradish forever, and it doesn't say anyone is disenfranchised if they find another way to feel it."

"Feel it." Martin set down his glass. "You want to feel it. That's very modern. Very hedonistic, actually, everything reduced to what you feel in the moment."

"Feeling something is the opposite of hedonistic," Priya said quietly, and Martin looked at her as though a chair had spoken.

The deadline, such as it was, arrived on schedule: Liam's little cousins had already vanished with the afikoman, and the Seder could not proceed until the hidden matzah was found and ransomed. Grandmother had decreed, as she did every year, that no one left the table during the search, which meant Liam had perhaps ten minutes of Martin's full attention, and Martin had spent twenty years guarding these ten minutes like territory. His uncle wanted the argument the way other men wanted the last word, and Liam understood, suddenly and uncomfortably, that this was why the argument kept happening. It was not really about the horseradish.

"It says the maror is eaten with the charoset," Liam went on, turning the pages, and here he was genuinely reading, his finger under the line, because he had promised himself he would not improvise. "The sweet with the bitter. Together. So even the rule, the actual rule, is not about suffering alone. It's about the mixture."

Martin was quiet for a moment. Outside, someone's car alarm went off and was ignored, as car alarms always were on this street.

"When I was your age," Martin said, "I told my father, your grandfather, that I didn't need the maror. I knew what bitterness was, I said. I was seventeen and certain." He turned his water glass a quarter turn, then another. "He made me eat the whole portion anyway. Extra horseradish. And I was furious for a year about it, maybe two. Now I make his portion every spring, and I don't know anymore whether I do it for him or against him."

Priya looked from one of them to the other. "So which is it?" she asked.

Martin smiled without any of his usual staging. "That, my dear, is above my pay grade."

From the hallway came a shriek of triumph: the afikoman had been found, wedged behind the coatrack, and the smaller cousin was already negotiating her ransom with a seriousness that suggested a future in law. The Seder lurched forward. Priya folded a piece of matzah into a small parcel with horseradish and charoset and put the whole thing in her mouth, and her eyes watered, and she nodded slowly, twice.

Liam did not think he had won the argument, if it could be called winning to have moved the question rather than answered it. He took his own portion, bitter and sweet together, and ate it while his grandmother counted heads and decided they were one short and then found she was wrong.

"Next year," Martin said, raising his glass toward Priya, "you're bringing the horseradish."

activity: to trace the steps of cellular respiration from glucose to ATP in the mitochondria
story:
The lab smelled of sulfur and floor wax, and Tyson had been staring at the same diagram for eleven minutes. Glycolysis, the citric acid cycle, the electron transport chain: arrows flowed across the page like a subway map, glucose dissolving into pyruvate at the top and ATP materializing at the end, inside a mitochondrion drawn as a fat bean. His exam was Monday. His grade in Biology 12 was balanced on the exam the way a coin balances on its edge, and his father had made the stakes plain enough that Tyson had felt the duress of it all week, studying under a lamp while his friends were out at the lake.

Across the bench, Priya was building a model of a mitochondrion out of clay, because she wanted the extra credit and, he suspected, because she wanted to be the kind of person who made things with her hands. She kept smoothing the inner membrane into folds, creasing them with the edge of a ruler. "Cristae," she said, when she caught him looking. "More folds, more surface area. Don't ask me why that matters yet, I haven't gotten there."

He hadn't gotten there either. He could recite the steps, glucose to pyruvate to acetyl-CoA, but the arrows went one direction on the page and nowhere at all in his head. He understood things better when he had to give them away, which was why, when his phone buzzed against the counter, he answered it even though he wasn't supposed to.

It was his cousin Drew, calling from the farm, where Drew spent the summers hauling feed and, apparently, wondering. "Tyson, that thing you said last month, about cells having instructions in them. Grandma's cows have the same kind of instructions as us?" Drew was fourteen and asked questions the way other kids threw rocks, casually and with force.

"Same kind, sure. It's called DNA." Tyson got up and walked to the window, away from Priya's careful folding.

"So when the cell needs to make something, it just sends the DNA out? Like mailing the recipe book to the kitchen?"

And here Tyson stopped, because the honest answer was that he didn't know, or rather that he had known in September and lost it somewhere. He had a vague image of a copy, a working copy, and he stood at the window trying to rebuild it. He remembered his teacher saying something about an enzyme, a machine that read the DNA without tearing it up, and he remembered the word polymerase surfacing in his mind the way a fish surfaces, briefly and then gone. Then it came back whole.

"No, actually. It's the opposite of mailing the book. The DNA stays where it is. There's an enzyme, it's called RNA polymerase, and it reads one strand of the DNA and builds a matching strand of messenger RNA. That's the copy. The messenger RNA carries the gene's instructions out to where the protein gets made."

"Why not just send the DNA?"

"Because you don't mail the original, I think. You keep the master safe and send a copy that can get wrecked in the mail." He said it and then heard it, and something turned over in him, some small gear catching. The cell kept its archive locked away and made a disposable working copy, and the whole thing ran on that division of labor.

When he hung up, Priya was remonstrating with her clay, poking at a fold that had collapsed, calling it obdurate as though the clay were a stubborn animal. He sat back down and looked at his diagram, and for the first time he saw the logic under the arrows, not a subway map but a supply chain, glucose broken apart because breaking things apart releases what they're holding, the released energy captured in small, spendable coins of ATP. The cell didn't get something for nothing. It traded, step by step, and every arrow was a price paid.

"I think I finally get it," he said. "Not memorize it. Get it."

"Get what?" Priya held up the bean, folded and lopsided, sunlight coming through the window and making the wet clay shine.

"Why the steps have to be steps. Why it doesn't just burn the sugar all at once. It's like the copy thing, it's all about control."

"You should explain it to me, then," she said, and pushed the diagram across the bench toward him. "Tuesday, after your exam. I'll bring the clay."

activity: to write and stage a ten-minute play about a moment from their own life
story:
Nathaniel's grandmother had turned her sunroom into a theater. That was her word for it, anyway, though the stage was a floral rug and the lighting was a dimmer switch she operated from behind the fern. He had come for two weeks in August to write a ten-minute play, one scene from his own life, and perform it for whatever relatives could be lured to the house with the promise of lemon cake.

The scene he chose was the morning his father drove him to the hospital to see his mother after her surgery, and how they had sat in the parking garage for forty minutes not talking, and how his father had finally told a story about a chicken. Nathaniel did not know yet that the story would be hard. He wrote the first draft in a single afternoon at the kitchen table, feeling briefly like a virtuoso, and printed it on his grandmother's ancient printer, which groaned like it resented every page.

The table read happened on Thursday. His cousin Priya came over, plus Priya's friend Marcus, who had done one summer of community theater and therefore considered himself an authority. Grandmother sat in her wicker throne with the script and a pencil, and Priya read the stage directions aloud in a news-anchor voice that made everything sound like a hostage situation.

They got through it. Marcus cleared his throat in the way people do before delivering a verdict. "The letter," he said.

"What letter?"

"The mom's letter. In the first scene. Nathaniel's dad pulls it out of the glovebox, and then it just never comes back. We never learn what's in it."

"It's a prop," Nathaniel said. "People have things in gloveboxes."

Marcus leaned back, delighted to have caught something. "My drama teacher calls that Chekhov's gun. Anton Chekhov, the playwright. Anything you clearly show on stage early should matter later in the play."

Grandmother looked up from her pencil. "In my day we called that foreshadowing, but I suppose guns are more dramatic than letters." She said this mildly, but Nathaniel felt it land like a verdict of her own. He had been caught, too, just less obnoxiously.

He argued for a while, because arguing felt easier than fixing it. The letter was atmosphere, he said. Real life was full of objects that never explained themselves. Priya pointed out that a play was not real life, it was real life boiled down, which was a sentence Marcus immediately claimed as his own. Then Priya, who could not help being fair even when Nathaniel was being a pill, said maybe the trouble wasn't the letter itself, it was that the scene seemed to think the letter mattered. The dad handled it, turned it over, put it back. The scene had aimed the gun and then forgotten it.

That night he sat in the sunroom with the dimmer switch at half, thinking about his mother's actual glovebox, which contained registration papers and a flashlight and eleven napkins from a sandwich shop that had closed years ago. He had made the letter up. He had put it there because a prop needed filling, and now the prop was demanding a reason to exist, like a guest who would not leave the party. There were two ways out, and he tried to hold them in his head at once. One was to cut the letter, which felt like losing something he could not name. The other was to let it come back, which felt like lying, because in the parking garage no letter had ever been read aloud.

He worked at it for two days. Cutting won, mostly. But he gave the chicken story a small extra beat, a callback the dad makes when they finally get out of the car, and Priya read that part again and said, "There. That's your gun. You just had it pointed at the chicken the whole time." Marcus objected that a chicken was not a gun, and Grandmother observed that Marcus's own performance of the dad had been penurious in its emotional range, which sent Priya into a fit of laughing and sent Marcus to the kitchen to sulk with the lemon cake, where he was quickly consoled by it.

On the day of the performance, the relatives arrived in force: two aunts, an uncle who clapped at the wrong moments, and Grandmother's neighbor Ruth, who had been promised cake and brought a folding chair in case of seating shortages. The sunroom held eleven people and one nervous playwright. Nathaniel had tried to forestall a crisis by taping down the rug's curled corner, and by deciding, at the last minute, not to play his father himself but to hand the role to Marcus after all, because Marcus did a better dad than Nathaniel could, and because Nathaniel had discovered he would rather watch the scene than be inside it.

It went well, mostly. Marcus forgot one line and invented a worse one, Ruth's chair collapsed during the parking garage silence in a long tin shriek, and in that strange shattered moment, with everyone frozen, Nathaniel's uncle said, "Well, that's garage ambience," and somehow it was. Afterward his aunts hugged him too hard and too long, and Priya said, "Ten minutes exactly, you absolute showoff," and Grandmother found him by the dimmer switch and put the pencil in his hand.

"Keep it," she said. "I marked all the places you cut too soon." He looked down at the margins, crowded with her small handwriting, and realized he would be coming back next summer whether or not anyone asked him to. "One more thing," she said, steering him toward the kitchen. "Ruth ate your piece of cake, and I need you to be brave about that."

story:
The line at the middle school gymnasium was longer than Mackenzie had expected, and she spent the first ten minutes of her adult life as a voter studying the back of a man's canvas jacket, a drawstring bag in her hand holding nothing but her driver's license and a granola bar. In October she would have been too young; in November she was not; the arithmetic of it still startled her, the way a door you had watched for years could open on an ordinary Tuesday.

When she reached the table, a volunteer with reading glasses on a beaded chain asked for her name so she could find it in the binder. Mackenzie slid her license across and said she had never registered anywhere, but here was her ID, and she was registered to vote in the sense that she was a citizen and eighteen. The volunteer's smile did something patient. "Honey, in this state you have to register before you can vote." Mackenzie felt her ears go hot. She had driven forty minutes from the dorms for this.

"There's no registration in North Dakota," she said, and heard how it sounded, like a claim about dragons. "I'm from Fargo. We just show up. You show ID and they check you off." The volunteer turned to a younger woman restocking pens, who leaned in with the mild delight of someone who actually knew something. "It's true. North Dakota's the only state without voter registration. They abolished it in 1951. You show identification at the polls instead." The older volunteer peered over her glasses at Mackenzie, no longer patient, something almost envious in it. "Huh," she said. "Fifty years I've run this table."

Mackenzie stepped out of line to text her father, thumbs clumsy in the cold air outside the doors. Turns out I can't vote today. ND doesn't register people so I never did, and here you have to do it in advance. She paused, then added, The deadline was three weeks ago. I thought being 18 was the deadline. His reply came while she was still standing there: You weren't wrong, exactly. You were North Dakota wrong. Then, a second message: My father voted every single year of his life and never once registered. Nobody made him. Go get coffee and we'll fix it for next time. Something in her chest loosened at we'll, though she was fairly sure she would be the one filling out the form.

She thought about her grandfather while she walked, because the word for what he had passed down was patrimony, even if what he had passed down was a habit: the Tuesday drive to the church basement, the pencil stubs, the little flag sticker he wore on his collar the rest of the day like a scout badge. She had assumed his ease was national, that the whole country worked the way his precinct did, and now she understood that his ease had been a kind of local luck. Two systems, one country. Hers had been the easy one, and she had not known it was luck until this morning.

Back inside, because she could not simply leave, she asked the younger volunteer whether there was anything she could still do. There was not, not for this election, but the woman walked her to a folding table near the exit and showed her the registration form, and Mackenzie filled it out standing up, printing carefully, using her dorm address and her mother's maiden name for the last four digits of her social. A querulous man behind her in the original line was complaining to anyone who would listen that the machines had been wrong last time, that his vote had been eaten, that nothing counted anyway. The older volunteer said, without heat, "Then why'd you wait in line, Gary?" and Mackenzie laughed before she could stop herself, and Gary, surprisingly, laughed too.

Outside, the sky had gone the flat gray that seemed to presage snow but never quite committed, and she sat on the low concrete wall by the flagpole and called her dad instead of texting. "Did you know?" she asked. "That it's just us? That literally no other state does it that way?" He said he had half known, the way you half know things about home, and that he should have told her when she moved, put it on the list with getting her oil changed. She told him about Gary, and the form, and the flag stickers, which her dad said they still gave out, in a box by the door, if you asked.

"So next year," her dad said. "You'll be ready." She said yes, and meant it, and also understood, sitting there with the uncast vote still in her like an unstamped letter, that ready was a word with more rooms in it than she had explored. She pulled her jacket tighter and walked to the parking lot, the completed form folded into thirds in her back pocket, its edge pressing against her hip with every step.

story:
The line outside the church hall on Delmore Street moved in short shuffles, and Brayden checked his wallet twice to be sure the voter information card was still there. His mother had worked polls for years and had habituated him to the ritual of elections, the sharpened pencils, the folded cardboard screens, but he had never been on this side of it. Today he was eighteen, registered, and carrying an argument he hadn't been able to settle in his own head all week.

Behind him, a girl about his age was talking to an older man in a quilted coat. "I thought you had to be twenty-one," she said. "My dad said he couldn't vote until he was older than us."

"Federal voting age," the man said. "Canada lowered it from twenty-one to eighteen in 1970." He said it the way people recite hockey stats, and then the line moved and he went back to his phone.

Brayden turned the number over. 1970. His grandfather would have been nineteen that year, suddenly eligible mid-decade, probably one of the first eighteen-year-olds in the family to mark a ballot. Brayden wished he could ask him, but his grandfather had been dead since Brayden was eleven, and the remaining memories were of a man who complained about taxes and grew dahlias, and who had once said, watching an election night on television, that young people vote like they're throwing rocks.

In front of him, two poll workers were laughing about someone's dog. One of them, a woman with reading glasses on a chain, noticed his card as he stepped up. "First time?" she said.

"Is it obvious?"

"You're holding it like a ticket that might not scan." She found his name on the list, folded the ballot into thirds without looking at it, and slid it across. "Straight to the box after."

The voting screen smelled of pencil shavings. Brayden stood there longer than he meant to. He had gone back and forth all week. His economics teacher, who liked to trace the etiology of every policy back to its first cause, had argued that the party promising lower costs would help his family most; his sister, home from university, had argued the opposite with equal force, and both of them had used numbers. The trouble was that he believed parts of each. He had started wondering whether a considered position was even possible, or whether everyone just picked a side first and built a bridge to it afterward.

His grandfather's line came back to him, throwing rocks. Maybe that was what 1970 had looked like to the people who already had the vote, a crowd of teenagers hurling something. Or maybe his grandfather had meant it as advice: don't vote to break things, vote to build one. Brayden noticed his own incipient bitterness, the itch to mark the ballot against whoever his father supported, purely because his father had been loud about it at dinner, and he recognized the feeling as not a reason. He put the pencil down for a second. Then he picked it up and marked the candidate he could actually defend out loud if someone asked him why, one whose platform he'd read twice and still had doubts about. The doubts were honest. He let them stand.

He fed the ballot into the box, and the poll worker with the glasses said, "There you go, citizen," in a tone that was half teasing and half not.

Outside, the girl from the line was waiting on the steps, scarf up to her chin. "Did you know it was only since 1970?" she said. "That people our age could vote. That's so recent. My dad voted at twenty-one and I voted at eighteen and nothing else changed."

"Something changed," Brayden said, though he wasn't sure what, exactly.

"Like what?"

He shrugged. "We're in the line now. We have to have an opinion even when we don't."

She laughed, a short sound that scattered into the cold. "I marked mine and I still don't know if it was right."

"That might be the whole thing," Brayden said. "Voting, I mean."

She pulled her scarf down so he could see her mouth. "You want to get coffee? There's a place on Delmore and I have forty minutes before my shift."

He looked back once at the church hall, at the box inside holding his folded answer, and then he zipped his coat. "Sure," he said. "I'm Brayden."

story:
The garage smelled of dust and old grass clippings, and Logan had claimed it for the weekend because the kitchen table was no longer negotiable. He was painting his grandfather's old tackle box, transforming the rusted green steel into something covered in koi, orange and white fish curling around the latch. He had promised it to his sister Nora before she left for her first semester, which was now four days away, and the deadline had begun to feel like a held breath.

He had learned two ways of thinking about a project like this from two different people. His grandfather, a machinist, believed in doing the thing once, correctly, with cleanup as part of the work itself. His art teacher junior year, an ebullient woman named Ms. Okafor, believed in momentum, in following an impulse before it cooled, and she had once told the class that a finished imperfect thing beat a perfect thing unfinished. Logan had spent a year treating those ideas as rivals. Now, with the tackle box half covered and Nora's departure looming, he was not sure they were rivals at all.

The trouble began on Saturday afternoon. He had thinned his acrylics with water all morning, rinsing brushes in a jar between fish, marveling at how easily the paint moved while it was wet. Then Nora called from inside the house, asking for help carrying bins to her car, and he set his three best brushes on the bench and went in. They hauled dorm bedding and a fan and four boxes labeled in her careful handwriting, and she thanked him with a hug that lasted longer than her usual ones, and by the time he got back, the sun had moved across the garage floor and two hours had gone.

The brushes were ruined. He picked one up and the bristles held their shape like a tiny frozen fan, stiff as a toothbrush found behind a radiator. He ran it under the tap and the water beaded off. The paint had been water-based all morning, thinning and rinsing like ink, and now it simply refused the water entirely, as if the brush had decided to become something else while his back was turned.

"You left them out," Nora said from the doorway. She had followed him back out with two mugs of lemonade, and she stood there looking at the stiffened brushes with an expression that was half apology and half diagnosis. "That happened to half my brushes last spring. Acrylic cleans up with water while it's wet, but once it dries, it won't. It just won't."

"I thought I had more time," Logan said.

"You thought a lot of things were more forgiving than they are." She set down the lemonade and picked up the stiffest brush, turning it over. "So what now?"

He sat on the stool and considered. His grandfather would have thrown the brushes away and said the lesson was the point. Ms. Okafor would have said the lesson was nothing next to the koi, and would have handed him a palette knife. He tried, for a moment, to historicize the problem, to imagine how his grandfather's generation of careful men would have judged a boy who abandoned his tools for a hug and a box of sheets. Then he stopped, because the judgment felt borrowed and useless. The brushes were stiff. His sister was leaving. Both of those were true at once, and the second one mattered more, and he was not going to pretend otherwise, even to look disciplined.

He worked the rest of Saturday and most of Sunday with the brushes that remained and a cheap flat brush he found in a drawer, its synthetic bristles coarse enough to leave visible streaks. The streaks, it turned out, looked like water. Where he had planned smooth gradients of white belly into orange scale, the stiff-bristled strokes made ripples, and the koi seemed to be moving. Nora came out Sunday evening in her socks, saw the finished box under the work light, and did not say anything for a long moment.

"You did that with the ruined brush?" she asked finally.

"The ruined brush and one from the junk drawer."

She ran her thumb along the latch, over a fish's eye. "It's better than the other way would have been, isn't it."

He wanted to say yes. He had a whole argument ready about mistakes becoming texture, about how a revisionist reading of the afternoon might call it luck instead of carelessness. But he genuinely did not know whether the streaks were better or whether he was only making peace with what he could not undo, and he found he did not want to hand her a tidy answer on her last night home. "I don't know," he said. "I like it. I'm still annoyed about the brushes."

Nora laughed, a short surprised sound, and tucked the tackle box under her arm like something she intended to keep forever. "Good," she said. "Bring the lemonade in when you come."

story:
The bowling alley smelled of rented shoes and cherry slushie, and Kaylee stood at the counter wondering whether she should pay for her own games before Dante arrived, or whether paying first would look like a statement. She had thought about it on the bus, weighing the two positions like a girl holding identical gifts in either hand. If she paid, she was independent, unbeholden; if she waited, she might seem to expect something. In the end she bought her shoes, rented two lanes by mistake, and had to ask for one lane back, which the clerk gave her with a look she chose not to interpret.

Dante came in at six exactly, which she liked, carrying nothing, wearing a jacket she had seen him in at school maybe four times and never once thought about until now. "You found it," she said, and he said, "I looked it up twice on the way," which she also liked, because it was an admission, and admissions were the currency she trusted.

He had asked her out on Tuesday, by the trophy case outside the gym, and she had said yes quickly, then spent the rest of the week deciding whether the quickness had been a mistake. Her mother, over dishes, had said only, "You don't owe anybody a second date, and you don't owe anybody a reason." Kaylee had rolled that around all week, and by Friday she had arrived somewhere adjacent to it: she didn't owe Dante a reason, but she might owe herself a fair look before making one up.

The first game, she won by nine pins. He laughed about it in a way that felt real, not performed, and she filed that away. On the second game, somewhere in the fourth frame, she noticed that they were both leaning on the ledge the same way, elbows down, chin on knuckles, watching her ball drift toward the gutter. She straightened up. A second later, so did he.

Her brother Will, home from his first semester of college, had told her about a study over winter break, in between complaints about his roommate. In a 1999 study, Tanya Chartrand and John Bargh had found that people liked a partner more when that partner quietly mimicked their posture and gestures, even without noticing the mimicry. Will had called it the chameleon effect, and Kaylee had filed that away too, the way she filed everything, in the drawer marked possibly useful, possibly nothing.

Now she watched. She crossed her ankles; two frames later his ankles crossed. She spun her cup in her hands; he got a cup of his own and spun it, laughing about something unrelated. And the strange thing was that she could not tell, watching him, whether it meant anything at all. If people liked a partner more when that partner mimicked them, then maybe he was doing it to be liked, which would be an affectation, a strategy, and she would have to decide how she felt about being managed. Or maybe it happened below everyone, some current neither of them steered, in which case there was no one to blame and nothing to decode.

"You're staring at your shoes," Dante said. "They're really something."

"They're size nines and they've been on four hundred feet."

"Mine have been on more," he said, and lifted one to show her, and she thought, without wanting to, he's matching me again, joking the way I joke.

By the eighth frame she had tried both ways of thinking and could not land on one. She tested him once more, deliberately, draping her arm along the ball return, and when his arm followed, thirty seconds later, she felt a small flat disappointment and a small warm spark at the same time, and could not have said which was the truer response. Maybe the study didn't cover this direction, her watching for it, both of them awake to the possibility. Maybe noticing ruined whatever the noticing was about.

She got a strike in the ninth, all ten pins folding sideways at once, and Dante stood up and held out his hand, palm up, noncommittal, offering the high five or something smaller, letting her choose. She looked at the hand. Her mother's rule said she owed him nothing; her own quieter rule said she owed him the truth of this moment, which was that she liked him and did not yet know why, and might not find out tonight.

She high-fived him, then kept her hand there a beat longer than the gesture required. "Overtime," she said. "Next game's mine to lose."

activity: to weigh two historians' differing explanations of the Cold War against the evidence
story:
Hunter spread the timeline across his grandfather's kitchen table, taping the last corner down while the coffee was still too hot to drink. Grandpa Frank wanted the counter cleared before lunch, and Hunter wanted the whole thing finished before Saturday, when he would have to stand in front of his class and defend a position he had not yet chosen. The assignment was simple on paper: two historians, two explanations of how the Cold War started, and the evidence weighed against each. Mr. Reyes had said, almost cheerfully, that either answer could earn an A, which struck Hunter as a way of making the choice harder, not easier.

Frank set down his mug and looked at the line of index cards. "You put the Long Telegram at the front."

"It's February 1946," Hunter said. "Kennan's cable from Moscow. That's where the containment idea starts. Historian number one, the one I read first, says that's the real beginning. Ideas before actions."

Frank tapped a card further along the strip. He had taught middle school geography for thirty-one years and had opinions about how maps, and apparently timelines, ought to be arranged. "And this one?"

"March 1947. The Truman Doctrine." Hunter read off his own card. "Truman pledged support for countries resisting communist pressure. Started with aid to Greece and Turkey."

"There's your beginning," Frank said.

"You always think it's whatever came after the war you were in."

"That's not fair," Frank said, but he didn't sound wounded; he sounded like he'd heard the argument before, in his own head, maybe. He sat down across the timeline so that it ran between them like a border. "A telegram is a man thinking. A doctrine is a country deciding. Which one changes what people do?"

Hunter hadn't expected his grandfather to take a side. He had expected him to make a sandwich and leave the table clear. Instead Frank pulled the Greek and Turkish cards toward himself and squared their edges, which was what he did with things he intended to keep talking about.

Historian number two, the revisionist, argued that the doctrine was the moment the United States stopped pretending and started building an empire of client states, that the rhetoric of freedom dressed up something colder. Historian number one called that cynical, said it valorized suspicion over fear, making a virtue of assuming the worst about your own country. Hunter had underlined that sentence twice and then felt embarrassed by the underlining, as if he'd taken a side by accident.

"Here's my problem," Hunter said. "If I say the telegram started it, then it's about ideas, and ideas are hard to prove. If I say the doctrine started it, then I have to decide whether the money for Greece and Turkey was defense or something worse. The evidence fits both."

"Then say so."

"That's a coward's answer."

Frank laughed, one short note. "I spent a spring in 1968 deciding whether to enlist. My father had a picture of Truman on the workshop wall his whole life, because of the doctrine, he said, because somebody finally drew a line. My brother called it an oligarchy with better manners, America deciding for other countries and calling it rescue. I stood between them at that table, the one we still have, and I said nothing, and they both walked away believing I'd agreed with them."

Hunter looked up from the cards. He had never heard this. The family story he knew was that Uncle Ray and Frank hadn't spoken much since the seventies, and nobody said why, and it had something to do with a girl before it had anything to do with politics.

"The telegram or the speech," Frank said. "You could do worse than to tell your class that the evidence supports both, and that the question of which came first depends on what you think a war is made of."

"It's made of money," Hunter said. "Six hundred million in aid, and nobody fired a shot over it."

"Somebody fired a shot over it," Frank said. "Just not in Greece." He stood, took his mug to the sink, and ran water over it longer than he needed to. "I'll be outside. Clear the table by noon."

Hunter worked for another hour. He moved the Long Telegram card half an inch left, then back. He wrote a sentence at the bottom of his notes, crossed out the first clause because it sounded turgid and dishonest, the kind of hedging that filled space without saying anything, and wrote instead: the doctrine is where the commitment became public and costly, and the telegram is where the fear first found its words, and the record does not settle which mattered more.

When Frank came back in at noon, smelling of cut grass, Hunter was rolling the timeline into a tube. "Well?" Frank said.

"I'll tell them the truth," Hunter said. "That I don't know where it started. Only where it stopped being somebody's opinion."

Frank took one end of the tube and held it while Hunter found the rubber band.

"Your great-grandfather would have argued with you till midnight," he said.

"Then I'd have been right where you were."
