story:
Abigail arrived early to claim the good seat, the one by the window, because today was the debate and she intended to win it. The question on the board read: Can a single experiment prove anything? She had argued all week with Marcus in the lab that one clean result was enough, that everything else was bureaucracy, and she had said it in a voice she privately knew was louder than the argument deserved.

Mr. Ferrell, whom Marcus called the last of the pedagogues, never lectured if he could make students collide instead, so he had set the room in two facing rows. Abigail opened her notebook to a page of prepared points. She remembered writing three of them last night, in order, with a heading. When she looked down, the page held only two, and the second one trailed off mid-sentence, as if her past self had fallen asleep mid-thought. She decided she must have written the third point on a different page, in the blue notebook, at home. She was almost sure of it.

"The Higgs boson," Marcus said, opening, and she felt the floor shift, because that was her third point, or something like her third point, and he had it now. "July 4, 2012. CERN announced it only after two separate detector teams found the same new particle." He paused, savoring the room's attention. "ATLAS and CMS. They worked independently. They didn't share their data first. Two giant detectors, same tunnel, same collisions, and neither team got to peek."

Abigail's rebuttal, which she delivered with more steadiness than she felt, was that this was waste, duplication, two machines where one would do. "If ATLAS saw it," she said, "why build a second one the size of a cathedral just to check?"

"Because a check is the whole point," said Priya from the back, and Mr. Ferrell wrote the word replication on the board without turning around, and under it he wrote peer review, and under that he drew nothing, just tapped the chalk twice.

The argument went on, but Abigail was no longer entirely in it. She kept thinking of her father, two summers ago, in the hospital corridor, when a single test had shown something on a scan and the doctor had said, gently, that they would run it again, differently, before anyone believed it. Her father had made a joke about being popular. Abigail had been furious, she remembered, at the delay, at the caution, at the refusal to just say what was true. She had told Marcus about it later and had told him the second test confirmed the first. She realized now, sitting in the third row by the window, that the second test had not confirmed it. She had said that to Marcus because it made a better story, a cleaner grievance against slowness, and she had repeated it to herself until it smoothed over into memory.

So when her turn came again, she did not use the rebuttal she had rehearsed. "I want to concede something," she said, and Priya mouthed the word concede with a sardonic lift of an eyebrow, and Abigail flushed but went on. "One result tells you something happened. It doesn't tell you it happened for the reason you think, or that it happens again. I still think two detectors is expensive. I still think July 4 is a showman's date for an announcement." She heard herself and stopped, because she was drifting toward a speech, and speeches were what she had accused Mr. Ferrell of all semester. "What I mean is, both things can be true. The caution is what makes it knowledge instead of news. But the caution costs something too. It's slow. Sometimes it's too slow for the people waiting on the answer."

Marcus looked at her across the rows. "So you're switching sides?"

"I'm not switching. I'm saying my side was thinner than I wanted it to be."

The bell would ring in four minutes and Mr. Ferrell would declare, as he always did, that no one had won, which was his way of winning. Abigail copied the three words from the board into her notebook, and under them she wrote her father's hospital and the date July 4, 2012, and then crossed out the hospital because it was not evidence, it was only her, and left the date.

After the others were gathering bags, she said to Marcus, quietly, "That thing I told you about my dad's second test. It came back different. I told you wrong."

Marcus zipped his bag. "Then what did they do after that?"

"They ran it again," she said, and looked at the empty board.

activity: to pass a driving test by practising parallel parking and merging on the highway
story:
The cones were laundry baskets, two of them, weighted with bricks and set along the curb of his grandfather's street at a distance Grandpa Ed had measured with his feet. "Pull up even with this one," Ed said, tapping the hood of his ancient Buick, "then turn the wheel all the way and back in slow." Michael had done it eleven times that week. He had clipped the baskets four times, kissed the curb twice, and once, on Thursday, slid the car in so cleanly that Ed had gone quiet for a moment before saying only, "Again."

The lease had come on Wednesday, forwarded from the apartment office in the college town, and Michael had read it at the kitchen table while Ed made tomato sandwiches. He had budgeted everything in the spring, back when the numbers had seemed solid: rent split with a roommate, a bus pass, food, books, a phone. The lease was thirty-one pages, and on page nineteen, under a paragraph about liability, he found a sentence that stopped him. He read it twice, then a third time, then carried the page to the counter.

"It says I have to carry renter's insurance," he said. "It covers my own belongings, not the building. It's not covered by what I'm already paying. It adds a monthly premium." He set the page down between the tomatoes and the salt shaker, feeling the arithmetic rearrange itself in his head before he'd done any of it.

Ed looked at the sentence over his glasses. "Renter's insurance," he said. "That's the one. Your grandmother had it on the duplex for years." He went back to the sandwiches and did not explain further, which was his way of leaving the problem where it belonged.

That night Michael sat on the foldout cot in the den with his notebook open to the budget page. Eleven dollars and change a month, the quote from the insurance website said. He looked at his columns. The bus pass was fixed. Books were a guess. The driving lessons, the ones Ed had been giving him since June with the quiet plan of a road test before September, were the only line with any give, and only because Michael had been paying for the practice permit fees and the gas out of his savings from the hardware store. It was not much. It was exactly the amount that was now spoken for.

He took the Buick out Saturday morning anyway. Ed rode in the passenger seat with the window down, one arm resting along the sill, and Michael parallel parked between the laundry baskets six times in a row without touching either one. On the seventh he overcorrected and flattened the rear basket with a plastic crunch. "You're looking at the cone," Ed said. "Look where you want the car to go." Michael pulled forward, reset the basket, and did it again, this time watching the space itself, the gap as a shape he was filling, and the car settled in near the curb with a foot of clearance. There was a strange pleasure in it, something almost like the pleasure of a solved equation, except that his hands knew it before his head did.

They took the highway after lunch. The on-ramp near the mall was short and curved, and merging had been the thing Michael feared most, the thing he'd had dreams about. Ed's method was arithmetic, not courage: "Match their speed before the lane ends. Watch the mirror, pick your gap, and don't slow down into it." The first merge was ragged. The second was worse; a sedan honked, and Michael's hands went cold on the wheel. On the third try he came up the ramp at sixty-five, found a gap between a box truck and a blue hatchback, and moved into it the way you'd slip into a conversation, matching the pace of the room. Nobody honked. Ed said nothing, which Michael had learned to read as the highest grade there was.

"I don't think I can pay for the road test this month," Michael said on the way back, taking the exit early because he'd seen the sign and decided without asking. "The insurance thing. It's every month, so it's not like I can wait a week and catch up. I found it in the lease and I should have found it before I signed."

"You signed already?"

"I signed in April. I just didn't read page nineteen." The exit ramp curved under the overpass, and he braked earlier than he needed to, checking the mirror twice. He understood now that there were two kinds of knowing things: the kind where you memorized the rule and executed it, like the parking, and the kind where you read the fine print of your own life and had to decide what to give up. He was not sure the second kind got easier. He suspected it did not, and that the best you could do was read everything twice.

Ed was quiet until the light at the bottom of the ramp. "You can take the test in October," he said. "The Buick isn't going anywhere." It was meant kindly. Michael heard the whole shape of it anyway: the freedom postponed, the cones gathering dust in the garage, the eleven dollars a month that would buy him, for four years, the protection of things he had not yet carried into a place he had not yet lived. The light turned green.

"Okay," he said, and drove his grandfather home the back way, the long way, past the school and the water tower, both hands on the wheel.

activity: to analyse the sonata form of a Mozart movement by marking its exposition, development and recapitulation
story:
James arrived early, as he always did, because the walk from the bus stop ran past the river and because Ms. Aldous's studio was the quietest room he knew. It was an almost ascetic space, one upright piano, one chair, a metronome she never turned on, and a shelf of scores with cracked spines. Today's score was Mozart's Sonata in F, K. 332, first movement, and his assignment was to mark the exposition, the development, and the recapitulation with colored pencil before his lesson.

The problem was that the boundary lines kept moving. He had circled a passage on page two, certain it opened the development, and then a phrase later he heard what sounded like the first theme returning, which would mean the recapitulation had arrived absurdly early, after barely a page. He erased the circle. He drew it again three bars later. Then he erased that one too, and the paper was turning gray where the graphite had been, as if he were trying to exhume the form from under his own mistakes.

Priya was there too, waiting for her own lesson in the hallway with the carpet that smelled of rain. She was sixteen as well, but a year behind him on the instrument, and she had spent the week composing rather than practicing, which was why her teacher was going to be annoyed with her. When James came out to drink from the water fountain, she waved him over and spread her manuscript notebook on her knee.

"Listen, math person," she said. "I wrote this melody and I know how it goes, but I don't know what time signature it's in. Some of my bars feel wrong."

He looked at her notebook. She had written a tune in E minor, and she had tried to box it into barlines, but the boxes did not agree with each other. He tapped the second bar and counted the note values with his finger, quarter notes and an eighth-note pair. "Five beats in this bar," he said. He counted the next one. "And five in this one. But this bar has four, and this one has six."

"So what time signature is it in?" Priya asked.

James started to say he didn't know, and then stopped, because he did know how the system worked, the way you know a fact only when someone asks you to use it. "The top number gives the number of beats in each bar," he said slowly, "and the bottom number gives the note value that gets one beat. So 4/4 means four quarter-note beats." He traced her first bar again. "If your bottom number is four, each quarter note is one beat, and your bars are telling you the melody is sometimes in five and sometimes in four and sometimes in six. It isn't in one time signature at all. Not the way you've written it."

Priya stared at the page as though it had betrayed her. "But it sounds right when I sing it."

"Then maybe the barlines are wrong and the melody is right," James said, and even as he said it, something shifted in him, a small gear catching. He had been treating the Mozart as though the form lived inside the barlines, as though the exposition ended wherever a phrase happened to stop. But the form was more like Priya's melody, something that flowed across the containers rather than filling them. The barlines counted the beats; they didn't decide the argument.

Back inside the studio, Ms. Aldous took the score from him and looked at his colored marks, the gray ghosts of erased circles underneath. "Tell me where your development begins," she said.

"Here," James said, pointing to the F sharp minor passage, "but I'm not certain. I found it by listening for the moment the music stops settling and starts pushing. The first theme keeps getting interrupted, pulled into keys it doesn't belong to. That's when I stopped trusting the barlines and started counting phrases instead."

Ms. Aldous played the passage he had marked, then played it again, and the sound filled the small room, running and uneasy, the left hand churning under the right. James listened with his eyes closed. The return of the first theme, when it finally came, in F major again, felt like an externality, something that arrived from outside his system of counting and instantly changed the value of everything he had marked before it. He opened his eyes. "There," he said. "That's the recapitulation."

"Almost certainly," she said. "Though Mozart plays games at exactly this point in his life, and there are movements where he shows you the theme in the wrong key first, just to take it away again. So hold your pencil lightly." She handed the score back and looked at Priya's notebook, which James had left on the piano lid. She opened it, and her eyebrows went up at the mismatched bars.

"Who told you it needed a time signature at all?" she asked Priya, who had drifted in from the hallway.

"My math person," Priya said, pointing at James, who had spent the entire week insisting that music obeyed rules you could count.

James opened his mouth to protest, and Ms. Aldous turned back to the Mozart, tapping the passage he had circled. "Play this for me," she said, "and while you play, count the beats out loud."

story:
Michael had been waiting eleven minutes with a laminated application under his thumb when his cousin Danny called from Montana, which was unusual, because Danny only called when he wanted something.

"You can get fired for having a bad mood," Danny said, without hello. "I'm telling you, Tyson got fired Saturday just for arguing with the manager."

"Not here," Michael said, stepping toward the window of the coffee shop so the espresso machine wouldn't drown him out. "Here they can fire you for anything. Bad mood, good mood, no reason at all."

"That's what I said. But Tyson's dad says no, that's illegal, and now it's a whole thing at Thanksgiving." Danny paused. "Where are you?"

"Getting a job, actually. I'll call you back." He hung up before Danny could laugh, though he could hear the laugh already assembling itself on the other end.

The manager, a woman named Rosa with a pen tucked behind each ear, had told him to fill out the form and she'd be over when the rush died. The rush had not died. Behind the counter a boy no older than Michael steamed milk with the grim concentration of someone performing surgery, and every third customer ordered something with a name like a password. Michael filled in his availability, which was all of it, and under previous experience wrote none, which felt like confessing to a crime.

He'd worked one shift before, technically. Last summer their neighbor Mrs. Okafor had paid him to repaint her porch, and he'd spent eight hours learning that the railings were older than his mother and just as set in their ways. He'd come home with paint in his eyebrows and forty dollars and a strange satisfaction he hadn't been able to name, something to do with a task that stayed finished when you finished it. School never stayed finished. School was a substance that regenerated overnight. His father called this a good work ethic and his sister called it asceticism, but she'd also once called breakfast cereal sectarian, so her vocabulary was not to be trusted entirely.

Rosa came over wiping her hands on a towel. "Michael, right? You're eighteen?"

"Yes. I start at State in the fall, so I wanted something for the summer. And maybe weekends after."

She looked at the form, then at him. "You know the pay is minimum, the work is dishes, and the espresso machine will try to kill you at least once."

"I'm fine with all three."

"Here's the thing," she said. "First ninety days you're on probation. After that it gets harder for me to let you go. I need a real reason." She said it flatly, the way you'd recite a policy, and moved on. "You can start Tuesday, six a.m."

He thanked her, and only after she'd turned back to the register did the shape of what she'd said settle on him. Probation. A real reason. He took out his phone and typed can a boss fire you for any reason and read, in the pale glow of a search page, that in most of the country the answer was yes, and then, further down, the exception: Montana. Montana was the one state where, after a probationary period, an employer generally needed good cause to fire a worker, under its 1987 Wrongful Discharge from Employment Act.

He called Danny back. The shop noise rose around him, dishes and steam and someone's complicated order being repeated for accuracy.

"Tyson's dad is right," Michael said. "Montana's different. It's the one state where, after a probationary period, your employer generally needs good cause to fire you. They made a law for it. The Wrongful Discharge from Employment Act, 1987."

"Since when do you know things?"

"I'm holding the internet. Also I just got hired, and apparently I get a probationary period too, so Tyson's situation depends entirely on what state he was standing in when he argued with his manager."

"Then it's a whole thing about geography," Danny said. "That's worse."

"Way worse." Michael watched the boy at the espresso machine extract a shot with the tenderness of a man defusing it. There was something he couldn't quite reconcile: the fact that a law could draw a line around a mood and call it protected, on one side of a border and not the other, and the fact that Rosa had told him about probation like she was handing him both a shield and a dare. He didn't know yet whether ninety days of arriving at six a.m. augured anything beyond ninety days of arriving at six a.m. He supposed he'd find out the way Tyson had, or wouldn't.

"Tell Tyson to move," Michael said, and pocketed the phone as Rosa waved him back over to the counter.

The office smelled of burnt coffee and toner, and Charles had been parked at his mother's spare desk since ten in the morning, charged with one task: run a report on the customer database while his mother was in back-to-back meetings. He had the query open on her second monitor, a thing of modest ambition. Select every account where the cancellation field had been left blank. He typed WHERE CANCEL_REASON = NULL, hit execute, and watched the database return nothing at all, zero rows, though he could scroll through the table himself and see the empty cells stretching out like an unpainted wall.

He assumed he'd broken something. He checked his semicolons, checked his spelling, ran it three more times, then leaned toward the next cubicle, where Dana from operations was eating sunflower seeds with the concentration of a man defusing them one at a time.

"Quick question," Charles said. "Is the database down, or am I?"

Dana rolled his chair over, read the screen, and did something worse than laughing. He smiled slowly and said, "Run it exactly like that again and watch the row count."

"I did. It's zero."

"Mm," said Dana, and rolled back to his seeds.

Charles sat with the insult of it. He opened the documentation himself, typed the comparison into the search box, and there it was, stated flatly: comparing anything to NULL with equals never returns true, and NULL = NULL doesn't either. You have to test with IS NULL. He read it twice, changed one line, ran it, and eleven thousand rows flooded the screen. He turned around to say something triumphant and found Dana already watching him with the expression of a man who had won a bet with himself.

"That's a stupid design," Charles said.

"That's a Tuesday," said Dana.

While the report exported, Charles picked up his phone, because at eighteen he could not sit in a chair for four minutes without it. His group chat had gone quiet and then loud all at once: a video, shared by his friend Ravi, of a river bursting its banks, brown water hauling a car sideways through a street, captioned with the name of a town two hundred miles from Charles's city and the word NOW. Below it, Ravi had written, "my cousin lives there, should I call her." Three people had already typed variants of oh my god.

Charles's thumb hovered over the share arrow. He caught himself thinking of the water as if the clip were the whole town, one street standing in for everything, a kind of synecdoche that videos always committed and viewers always forgave. His mother, from the doorway of her meeting, had once put it more bluntly: "Before you forward anything, check where it came from and when. You wouldn't repeat a rumor someone told you in an elevator without asking which elevator." She was not lecturing. She was holding two coffees and looking for the intern whose name she had momentarily lost, and Charles had nodded the way you nod at a thing you intend to do someday.

He did it now. He took a screenshot of a distinctive frame, the crooked sign above the flooded storefront, dropped it into a reverse image search, and waited while the results assembled themselves. The same footage, posted fourteen months ago, by a regional news account, about a different river entirely, in a different country's spring floods. The alluvial brown of the water was, apparently, a universal color. Ravi's cousin, Charles was fairly confident, was in no danger from this particular car.

He typed into the chat: "Hold on before you call anyone." Then: "It's from last year. Here." He pasted the link. There was a pause, the visible three dots of someone composing and reconsidering, and then Ravi answered, "oh. okay. good catch," followed by an apology emoji wearing a hard hat for no reason Charles could determine. A third friend, Marcus, tried to prevaricate, writing that the video "could still be happening somewhere like that," and Charles watched the sentence sit there, dishonest and lonely, until Ravi replied with a single "?" and Marcus sent, "fine, deleted."

Charles put the phone face down and looked at the exported report, at the eleven thousand rows that had been invisible to him an hour ago because he had asked his question in a way the database could not answer. It was the same error twice in one morning, he thought, and then declined to make too much of it, because he was not sure it was the same error, exactly, only that it rhymed. The video had been technically visible and wrong. The rows had been technically there and unread. He knew which mistake he'd rather be caught making, and he knew that knowing was not the same as never making it again.

His mother appeared at last, coffee-less, asking how the report had gone. Charles told her it was done, then added, "Also, Ravi almost called his cousin because of a flood video."

"Real flood?"

"Real flood, wrong year, wrong river."

She looked at him for a second longer than the fact required. "Good," she said, and then, because Dana was still watching from the next cubicle with his cup of seeds, "Dana, did you teach him that equals NULL thing or did you let him suffer?"

"He suffered," Dana said happily, and pushed the cup across the divider toward Charles.

activity: to explain how greenhouse gases trap heat and read a graph of carbon dioxide over the last century
story:
The training room behind the planetarium's projection dome smelled of dust and old carpet, and Eric sat at the far end of the table with the graph of atmospheric carbon dioxide printed twice, once for himself and once for whoever wandered up to his station on Saturday. He was sixteen and had volunteered because his mother had said, gently, that he needed something besides his bedroom. The outreach coordinator, Dana, had handed him a sheet of talking points and told him to make the science his own, which was the sort of instruction that sounded easy and was not.

"Explain it to Priya first," Dana said, nodding toward a college sophomore in a museum windbreaker who was rolling extension cords. "If she understands you, the public will."

Priya dropped into the chair across from him and put her boots on the rung. "Go ahead. Dumb it down."

"Okay." Eric flattened the graph. The line began low and level, then bent upward after the middle of the century, climbing in a curve that looked almost graceful if you forgot what it measured. "So the sun sends light through the air, and the ground sends heat back up. Some gases, like carbon dioxide, let the light through but catch the heat on the way out. The more of them there are, the more heat sticks around." He traced the curve with his finger. "This is the amount in the air, year by year. See where it stops being flat."

"Where it stops being flat," Priya repeated. "That's a good phrase. Say exactly that." She turned the paper sideways, squinting. "Why is it jagged, all those little teeth?"

Eric looked at the sawtooth pattern riding on the climb and admitted he didn't know yet. Dana, passing behind them with a ladder, said only, "Look it up before Saturday," and kept walking.

He looked it up that night at the kitchen table, and the teeth turned out to be the planet breathing, the forests and the plankton inhaling and exhaling each year while the whole curve rose beneath them, a rhythm stacked on a trend. He read longer than he meant to. His father came in from the late shift and stood behind him, reading over his shoulder the way he used to when Eric was small, before the year they had stopped talking about anything important. His father worked at the plant east of town, the one the governor had promised to protect, and they had an unspoken amnesty in the house on the subject of energy, a truce neither of them had ever proposed aloud. Tonight his father just said, "Teeth like that, you could teach me poker," and went to bed.

Saturday came, and the planetarium filled with families escaping the heat. At Eric's station there was a lightbox showing ocean currents overlaid on a map of the Atlantic, part of a new exhibit Dana had borrowed from the university. A boy about nine stood in front of it, frowning, dragging his finger along a red thread of water.

"That one's the Gulf Stream," the boy announced. "But the label changes." His finger crossed a point east of the Grand Banks of Newfoundland. "Is it a different river?"

"No," Eric said, and then, because he had spent Thursday evening with the map and the exhibit notes while everyone else left, "past the Grand Banks of Newfoundland, where it heads toward Europe, it's called the North Atlantic Current. Or the North Atlantic Drift." He said it the way he'd practiced, matter-of-fact, the way Dana said the names of stars. "Same water, new name."

"The ocean just changes its mind?"

"People change what they call it," Eric said. "The water keeps going." The boy seemed satisfied by this and moved on to the shark display, and Eric stood there for a second longer than he needed to, because the sentence had landed somewhere in him that had nothing to do with oceans. He had spent a year trying to codify his family's politics into something he could argue, positions with edges, and the argument he'd finally had with his father had been clean and terrible. His father believed in the plant the way you believe in a person. Eric believed in the graph. Somewhere between the two there was a fact that had not changed its nature, only its name, and he did not yet know what to call that.

At noon his phone buzzed with a message from his father, unusual enough that he stepped into the corridor by the restrooms to read it. "Saw the paper says this July is the warmest on record for the state. Your mother says you're doing the climate table at the planetarium. Tell me about the graph sometime. Not to fight. I'll bring coffee." Eric read it twice. The feeling it produced was inchoate, part anger, part something softer he had no word for, and he pocketed the phone without deciding what to reply, because a woman with two small children had just stopped at his table and the older child was pointing at the lightbox.

"Is that the Gulf Stream?" the woman asked.

Eric set the graph of carbon dioxide beside the ocean map, the rising curve and the red thread of warm water crossing toward Europe, and turned them so both could see. "It is," he said. "And farther east it's called the North Atlantic Drift. Same water, new name. Let me show you what it's been doing to the air."

activity: to interpret a blood pressure reading and explain how diet and exercise change it
story:
Lea set the cuff on the kitchen table between the butter dish and her grandmother's crossword, and Grandma looked at it the way she looked at the dentist's appointment card on the fridge, which was to say with total denial. "It's just a number," Grandma said, filling the kettle. "Doctors like to pathologize everything now. In my day you had a heart and that was that."

"That's literally the opposite of learning," Lea said. She had promised her mother she would figure this out before her college interview on Saturday, which was for a health sciences program and which would apparently include a station where she had to take a reading and then explain, out loud, how diet and exercise change it. Her mother had handed her the cuff like a gauntlet. Her grandmother was the practice patient, drafted that morning over toast.

Grandma sat down because Lea pushed the chair out behind her knees, and held out her arm like a woman donating blood under protest. The first number came up high enough that Grandma said "hah" in a tone of vindication, and Lea felt something in her chest go tight and defensive, because the number was hers to explain now and she did not want it to be bad news. She wrote it down anyway, in the notebook with the flamingo on the cover, and then stalled by rewrapping the cuff with great ceremony.

The second reading was lower. Not by a little. Lea looked at the two numbers, then at her grandmother, who was sitting with her ankles crossed and her elbow propped on the table below the level of her heart, chatting about the neighbor's hedge. Something was wrong with the picture, and it was not, Lea was fairly sure, her grandmother's circulatory system. She flipped the cuff box over and read the little folded instruction sheet she had skipped that morning in her confidence, the way she skipped recipe steps and then wondered why the cake collapsed. Feet flat on the floor. Sitting quietly for about five minutes first. Arm supported at heart level. Posture and activity change the numbers. She had marched Grandma in from the garden, sat her down, and pumped immediately, like a customs officer.

"We're doing it wrong," Lea announced. "Not you. Me. You have to sit still for five minutes first. Feet flat. Arm up here." She stacked two cushions and lifted the machine onto them, then slid a phone book under the table leg that wobbled, feeling like an engineer and a fraud simultaneously. Grandma, who had spent thirty years telling Lea to sit still, found this hilarious and began narrating in a golf-announcer whisper. "She remains motionless. The crowd holds its breath."

Lea set a timer. Five minutes was longer than she expected when you weren't allowed to talk, so she talked anyway, quietly, mostly to herself, about the interview. "They'll ask me how exercise lowers it and I'll say, well, the heart gets more efficient, and regular aerobic exercise tends to bring the numbers down over time, and diet, less salt, more vegetables, the stuff you already do, and they'll nod." Grandma, staring fixedly at the ceiling in exaggerated patience, said, "You sound like a pamphlet. Say it like you're talking to a person."

It had happened once before, Lea realized, and she'd missed it. Two weeks ago at the pharmacy, a girl from her chemistry class had rushed in off her bike, used the machine by the blood pressure aisle, and gasped at the number like it was a test grade. Then she'd sat on the bench to text her mother about it, feet flat, arm forgotten, and tried again before leaving, and the second number had been much lower, and Lea had thought nothing of it except that the machine was probably cheap. The girl had walked out calm. The machine hadn't changed. The five quiet minutes had.

The timer went off. Lea took the reading with her grandmother's arm resting on the cushion, supported, at heart level, and the number came back down in the ordinary range, and Grandma said, "See? A healthy woman," and Lea said, "See? a correct measurement," and they were both right, which was the annoying part. In her notebook she wrote the three numbers in a column and then, underneath, the rule in her own words: sit quiet five minutes, feet flat, arm at heart level, because posture and activity change the numbers. Then she crossed out "pamphlet" and rewrote her explanation of diet and exercise the way she'd say it to a person, which turned out to be mostly the same words in a different order, with a joke about Grandma's salt shaker.

"One more," Grandma said, settling back into the cushions like an aesthete who had decided blood pressure monitoring was a nascent art form and she its first great model. "I like the quiet part." She closed her eyes. Lea pressed start.

activity: to compose a sixteen-bar melody with chord changes and write it in standard notation
story:
The practice room smelled like resin and old radiator dust, and Hannah had the piano bench to herself until three-thirty, when the jazz combo would claim it for the rest of the afternoon. She had ninety minutes and a blank staff paper. The assignment, due Friday, was a sixteen-bar melody with chord changes, written in standard notation, and she had spent two evenings on it without producing anything she could stand to play twice. Mr. Okafor had said the second attempt was always better than the first, which was a comfort only if you finished a first attempt.

She had a first half. Eight bars in C minor, four bars of a tune that walked down and four bars that answered by climbing back, i and iv and V and i, and she thought the phrase had a certain modularity, four bars that could stand alone or lean on the four that followed. That was what she liked about tonal music: pieces built out of blocks that clicked together. But the back eight kept collapsing. Everything she wrote after the double bar sounded like the front eight wearing a different hat.

Marcus knocked on the door frame with his knuckle, headphones around his neck, laptop under his arm. He had the same assignment. "Are you writing it or staring at it?"

"Both," Hannah said. "Sit down and be useful."

He set the laptop on the piano lid and opened his listening log. They had a quiz next period on the Beethoven sonata, the one in C minor, and Marcus had a way of studying that involved pacing, so he paced the length of the practice room with one earbud in. Hannah played her eight bars while he walked. He stopped at the window.

"That's decent," he said. "Actually decent. What's the B section do?"

"Nothing yet. That's the problem."

He pulled out his own staff paper, covered in erased smears, and played her phrase back from memory, wrong in two places but wrong in a way that sounded almost better. Then he went back to his earbud, mouthing along, and Hannah watched his face do something odd, a small frown of disagreement, like he was arguing with the recording.

"Wait," he said. "Play track four."

She closed her staff paper and took his other earbud. The first theme came in, heavy, low, unmistakably dark, and then the music opened out and the second theme began, and it was as if someone had turned all the lamps on in a house that had been shuttered. Hannah heard it and, without knowing why, felt her whole body ease.

"That's it," Marcus said. "That's the second theme. But hold on, I wrote in my notes that the second theme goes to the dominant. G major. That's what I said for the quiz."

"It's not G major," Hannah said. She picked out the new key's notes on the piano, hunting for the triad underneath the tune. E-flat, G, B-flat. "It's E-flat."

"E-flat major in a C minor movement." He said it slowly, like he was setting stones. "So my notes are wrong."

"Your reasoning is wrong, or the piece is an exception." She thought of the tonic triad of C minor, the E-flat already sitting inside it, the most ordinary note in the world, suddenly promoted to a whole key. She pulled her theory workbook out of her bag and flipped to the chapter they'd skimmed, the one on form, and there it was in a table she'd never read closely: in a minor-key sonata-form movement, the exposition's second theme usually moves to the relative major. E-flat was the relative major of C minor. She turned the book so Marcus could see.

"Relative major," Marcus said, and wrote it in the margin of his listening log, hard enough to emboss the next page. "Okay. So the quiz answer is the relative major, not the dominant. I would have missed that."

"You owe me," Hannah said, but she was barely paying attention to him, because her hands were already back on the keys. Her front eight was in C minor. The back eight could do what Beethoven did: it could move to E-flat major. It could turn the lamps on. She played her first phrase again and then, without letting herself hesitate, pushed the melody up to land on E-flat, and the B-flat and the G fell into place around it like something that had been waiting in the room the whole time.

It wasn't a quotation. The rhythm was hers and the contour was hers, the descending four bars still walking down but now in a brighter country, and the answering phrase climbed through the new key's chords instead of the old ones. It was ordinary of her to do this, she knew that; a million students in a million practice rooms had written B sections that way, because the idea was in the air of every piece they'd ever heard. But hearing where it came from, hearing Beethoven make the same turn an octave lower and two centuries earlier, made the choice feel like a decision instead of a default. She was borrowing a way of thinking, not a tune.

"Play it all the way through," Marcus said.

She played all sixteen bars. The turn to E-flat still surprised her a little each time, and she hadn't decided whether the surprise was the point or a flaw, whether a listener should feel the ground shift or should be carried over it without noticing. She didn't know yet. She wrote the E-flat chord symbols in pencil above the back eight, lightly, so she could change her mind.

"How do you notate the F in bar twelve," Marcus said, leaning over her shoulder. "Sharp or natural?"

"Natural. Here, look."

She drew the note herself, stem up, and played it twice to prove it.

activity: the idea of opportunity cost, that choosing one thing means giving up the next best alternative
story:
Audrey had been at Dale's Auto for two hours, and the sedan she wanted had grown no cheaper in that time, only more familiar, like a dog at the shelter she was afraid someone else would take home. She ran her thumb along the hood's edge while Mr. Kessler, the salesman, talked about financing in a voice pitched to sound like a favor between friends. The price was eleven thousand dollars used, and she had nine saved from two summers bussing tables, plus what her grandmother had sent for graduation, which was supposed to be for textbooks.

Her phone buzzed against her hip. It was her friend Dev, and she stepped between a row of pickups to take it.

"I'm not quitting," Dev said before she'd finished saying hello. He worked at the pharmacy on Route 9, and he'd hated it since October, when they'd changed his schedule and stopped letting him sit down. "I already bought the uniform. Eighty bucks. Scrubs, the jacket, the shoes. If I quit now, that money's gone for nothing."

"That money's gone either way," Audrey said. "It's gone. You spent it in October."

"You don't get it. I have to stay long enough for it to be worth it."

She looked through the dealership window at the little sedan, silver, dented once near the back wheel, and something about the shape of Dev's argument bothered her the way a word bothers you when you've spelled it wrong. She told him she'd call back and walked inside to the coffee station, where a retired couple was arguing pleasantly about whether to trade in their truck.

Mr. Kessler found her there. "You've been circling that Camry all afternoon," he said. "You know what I see? I see a young person who wants to be responsible. Tell you what. We can do the paperwork tonight, get you a student rate."

If she bought the car tonight, the money her grandmother sent would go into the loan instead of the campus bookstore. Without a car, she'd take the bus home at Thanksgiving and Christmas, and her mother would drive the forty minutes to campus every other Sunday with groceries and whatever news had happened since the last visit. With the car, she could come home whenever she wanted, or never. She stood at the counter where the paperwork waited in a neat folder, and she understood that whichever way she chose, a whole version of her life was being quietly cancelled, the way they cancel a flight, apologetically, with a voucher.

"It's called opportunity cost," she said to Mr. Kessler, mostly to herself, but he nodded as though she'd complimented the coffee. "Whatever I pick, the next best thing is the price."

"You're a sharp one," he said, which absolved him of having to listen.

She called Dev back from the lot, between the used sedans and a populists billboard demanding lower gas taxes. "Listen," she said. "I learned about this once. The Concorde fallacy. It's named after the British and French governments. They kept funding the Concorde airliner even after they recognized there was no economic case for it anymore. They'd spent so much already that they kept spending. It has a name because everybody does it."

"So my scrubs are a supersonic jet."

"Your scrubs are a supersonic jet."

There was a pause, and she heard a register beep in the background, and then Dev said, "I'll think about it," which she recognized as an equivocal answer, the kind that lets a person keep the uniform in the closet a few more weeks.

Inside, the retired couple had signed for a smaller car than the truck, and the husband was explaining to Mr. Kessler that the truck money was going toward their granddaughter's tuition, and the wife was saying they'd miss the truck, and both things were true at once and neither was wrong.

Audrey sat down across from Mr. Kessler and slid the folder toward her, then didn't open it. "Not tonight," she said. "I want to think about the bus."

"The bus," he repeated, with a smile she could tell he'd use on the next kid.

Walking out, she passed the Camry one more time and patted its fender, feeling righteous, feeling like someone who had dodged a fallacy, someone who understood that money already spent could not be recovered and choices should be made forward, not backward. She was still feeling that way when she reached the road and checked her phone: a text from her mother, sent an hour before. She had taken a job in Phoenix. She'd been waiting until Audrey decided about the car to say it, because if Audrey bought the car, she wouldn't need rides anymore, and Phoenix was far, and the decision had been made, her mother wrote, for a while now.

Audrey stood in the parking lot with the dealership lights going out behind her, one by one, and the empty spot where the silver Camry had been.

activity: to compute the electric field strength at a point between two charged plates
story:
The problem sheet had been in Taylor's back pocket through the whole school day, folded twice, and by the time she reached the playground behind her brother's elementary school the paper was soft at the creases. She sat on a swing that still had morning dew on the chains and smoothed the sheet against her thigh. The problem gave the charge on each plate of a parallel-plate capacitor, the area of each plate, and nothing else. It asked for the field strength at the midpoint. Taylor read it three times, then turned it over, as though the back might contain the missing voltage.

Her brother, Marcus, was across the sand with two boys from his class, negotiating a turn on the climbing dome with the gravity of a trade delegation. That was the arrangement: she watched him for an hour until their mother got home from the deposition she had to give downtown, and in exchange she had the hour. Usually she spent it on her phone. Tonight the unit test was tomorrow, and the unit was electrostatics, and the unit was not going well.

The formula she knew best was E equals V over d, voltage divided by plate separation. She knew it the way she knew her locker combination, without having to think, and that was the problem. It was so familiar that it felt like the only door. She wrote it at the top of her scratch paper anyway, then sat with the swing ticking faintly behind her, chains settling, and looked at what she actually had. Charge. Area. Not separation, not voltage. The formula wanted things she had not been given, and would not give back anything in return.

"Taylor, watch this," Marcus called. He hung by his knees from the low bar, shirt over his face, arms dangling. She raised a hand without looking up. One of his friends said something about the clouds, which were moving fast, a mercurial gray mass shoving itself across the sky, and she registered this only because if it rained the paper would be ruined.

She had a memory of the second formula, not from the textbook but from the lecture, and the memory was mostly of Professor Alabi's handwriting, which slid downhill across the whiteboard. Something equaled charge per area divided by a constant. She had not written it down. She had assumed the voltage version would cover her, because it always had before, and now she was sitting on a damp swing with half a formula and a test in nineteen hours.

The reading was on her laptop at home, page 614, and she had not brought the laptop because she had promised herself an hour outside. She texted Dana instead. Dana was in the study group, the one that met without Taylor, the one Taylor had stopped going to after the first session because everyone there seemed already enfranchised in a way she wasn't, speaking the material like a first language. Taylor typed: do you remember if there's another way to get E for plates. She typed it and did not send it for a full minute, thumb hovering, sand cool against her sneaker soles, the smell of it mineral and faintly wet.

She sent it. Dana's reply came while Marcus was arguing about whose turn it was: yeah sigma over epsilon nought. Taylor stared at the words. Sigma was charge per area, that much she could assemble, dividing the charge on a plate by the plate's area. Epsilon nought was the constant, the permittivity of free space. Dana's next message read: it's about 8.85 times 10 to the minus 12 farads per metre. No voltage needed. Taylor read that twice. No voltage needed. The problem she was holding was not broken. It was written for exactly this route, and she had spent two days convinced it was a typo.

She worked it on the scratch paper, pressing hard enough that the letters showed through to the back. Charge divided by area, then divided by that tiny constant, the decimal swimming, and out of it came a field strength, a real number with a real unit, the field at the midpoint and in fact everywhere between ideal plates. She checked it against a sample problem she remembered from class, the right order of magnitude, and felt something in her shoulders let go. She texted back: thank you. Then, because it cost her something and she paid it anyway: I should come to study group. Dana sent a thumbs up and the time, 7 tomorrow, which was after the test, but there was the next one, and the one after that.

"Taylor." Marcus was standing in front of her with sand in his eyebrows. "It's spitting." The first drops were darkening the fold of the problem sheet, and she put it inside her jacket, against her chest, and stood up. The playground was emptying, mothers calling children in from the slides, the chains of the other swings ticking in a small wind. Marcus took her hand without being asked, the way he had since he was small, and she let him, the worked problem riding with her under her jacket, dry.

activity: to explain consent, contraception and how to get tested for infections at a clinic
story:
The clinic on Marsh Street closed at four, and Maya's bus back to her mother's house left at five, which gave them one hour and a grandmother's kitchen in which to figure everything out. Layla set her phone on the table between a bowl of runner beans and a plate of metamorphic rock slices her grandfather had collected in the Ozarks, pressure and heat written into their banded faces, and she thought that was as good a description of the past month as any.

"You can't tell Mom," Maya said. She was sixteen and had her jacket on already, though the bus was an hour away, as if she might have to run.

"I'm not telling anyone. That's the whole point." Layla had promised herself she would do this right, that she would be the older cousin she'd needed at sixteen and never had. Health class had given her the words, and AP Bio had given her the framing, the idea that the body keeps itself balanced, maintains its homeostasis, and that knowing how to protect that balance was not shameful but practical. Still, saying the words aloud to Maya's face was different from writing them in a notebook. She wiped the table with a cloth, an old habit at their grandmother's, burnishing the wood to the dull shine it always kept, and made herself start.

"Okay. First, consent. It's not the absence of a no. It's the presence of a yes, out loud, from someone who knows they can change their mind and it still counts." She kept her voice level. "If you're unsure at any point, you stop. That's not ruining anything. That's the rule working."

Maya nodded, chin down, picking at the hem of her jacket.

"Second, contraception. Condoms are the only ones that protect against infections, not just pregnancy, and they have to be on before any contact, not halfway through. If you want something longer term, the clinic can talk you through it, but tonight, condoms. And don't let anyone tell you they're too big. That's not a thing."

"Devon said that once," Maya said quietly.

"Then Devon can practice opening the wrapper until he gets humble about it." Layla watched a small grin cross her cousin's face and felt something in her own chest loosen.

"Third, testing. If you've already done something, or you're about to, you can get tested and treated without Mom signing anything. I'm almost positive. But almost positive isn't good enough, so we're calling before four." She pulled up the clinic's number, then hesitated with her thumb over the screen. Her own mother still reviewed her explanations for everything, and the instinct ran deep, that anything involving your body required a permission slip, a countersignature, an adult standing behind you. She dialed before the instinct could win.

The hold music was a tinny version of something she half recognized. Their grandmother drifted through for her reading glasses, paused at the tension around the phone, and set down a glass of sweet tea at Maya's elbow without a word before disappearing into the front room, and Layla was grateful in a way she didn't stop to examine.

"Marsh Street clinic, this is Renee."

"Hi. My cousin wants to come in for STI testing and she's sixteen. Does a parent have to sign a form?" Layla held Maya's gaze while she asked, because the question was hers too, had been hers for two years.

"All fifty states and Washington, DC, let minors consent to testing and treatment for sexually transmitted infections without a parent's permission," Renee said, in the tired, competent tone of someone who answered this forty times a week. "Some states do set a minimum age, so tell me which state you're in and we'll check."

Layla gave the state, listened, and wrote the walk-in hours on the back of a grocery receipt. When she hung up, she slid the paper across the table to Maya, who read it twice, as though the words might revise themselves.

"So I just walk in," Maya said.

"You just walk in. Before four today, or any Saturday morning." Layla reached over and straightened the collar of Maya's jacket, which had folded under itself, a small thing, but her grandmother had done it for her a hundred times and it meant stay, you're cared for. "And whatever happens with Devon, or doesn't, you don't owe me a report. You just get to be safe."

Maya stood, crumpling the receipt into her pocket with a kind of care, smoothing it flat again through the fabric. From the front room their grandmother called out that the 5:10 was unreliable and the 4:40 was worse, so they'd best leave now if they meant to make either.

Layla grabbed the keys off the hook by the door, and Maya was already on the porch, one foot on the first step, looking back.

story:
The scholarship application wanted two hundred volunteer hours, and Jackson had been counting his at St. Bridget's like a prisoner scratching tally marks on a wall. He had sixty-one. Today he was restocking the hydration station on the fourth floor, filling little green pitchers with ice and water, when he noticed that the family lounge outside Room 412 had gone quiet in the way rooms do when something heavy is being said.

"I want to be clear about the morphine," a doctor was saying through the half-open door. Jackson had seen her before, Dr. Reyes, the one with the gray braid who never used the elevators. "It will ease his breathing. That is what I intend. But at this dose, there is a chance it could shorten the time he has left. I want you to hear that from me and not from a nurse's note after the fact."

A woman's voice, thin and frayed: "So you're asking us to sign something that kills him faster."

"I'm asking you to let me treat his pain."

Jackson stood in the hallway with a pitcher sweating in both hands. He had assumed, without ever putting it into words, that doctors simply did good, the way furnaces simply produced heat. The idea that a good act could carry a foreseeable harm inside it, like a stone in a peach, was new, and he carried it with him down to the lounge where the patient's grandson sat hunched over an untouched coffee. Jackson only meant to be kind. He said that he'd overheard the doctors, that morphine could end things sooner, that maybe the family should fight it. The grandson's face changed, and he was through the door of 412 before Jackson had finished his sentence.

The charge nurse found him twenty minutes later and lambasted him in the supply alcice, her voice low and shaking, telling him that patient information was not his to repeat, that he had walked into the middle of a decision that had nothing to do with him. "The family's talking to a lawyer," she said. "If it goes anywhere, you could be part of a deposition. Sworn testimony, Jackson. About something you don't understand."

That night he sat on his bedroom floor with his phone and typed in what he remembered: harm you foresee but don't intend. The results led him to the doctrine of double effect, traced back to Thomas Aquinas, who had argued that causing a harm one foresees but does not intend can be permissible when it is a side effect of pursuing a good end. Jackson read it three times. Foresees, does not intend. The doctor hadn't been hiding anything from the family; she had been laying the whole trade on the table, the pain relief against the days it might cost, and asking them to weigh it. Jackson had taken the scale and thrown it at the grandson.

He asked to see the charge nurse before his next shift, and he told her he would say exactly what he had done, to the family, to a lawyer, to anyone, but that he had gotten the doctor's meaning wrong. Dr. Reyes was the one who came to find him instead, in the hallway by the ice machine. "I heard what you told them," she said. "You made it sound like we were choosing his death. What we were choosing was whether he spends his last days gasping or resting. Those are not the same conversation."

"I didn't know there was a difference," Jackson said.

"There is, and then there isn't," she said. "Aquinas gives you the frame, but the frame doesn't carry the weight for you. The family asked me yesterday whether the morphine was worth two days of his life. I said I couldn't answer that. Nobody can. We chose the morphine."

Mr. Okafor died four days later, on a Thursday morning, and the lawyer's letter never came, so there was no deposition, only a note in Jackson's file that his shifts would be supervised for the rest of the summer. His friend Diego texted him a picture from the lake, three girls on a dock, the caption calling it a hedonistic July, and Jackson typed "have one for me" and put the phone face down. On his last supervised shift, the grandson appeared at the fourth-floor desk, holding a paper bag of mangoes. "You stuck your nose where it didn't belong," he said, "but after you did, my mother finally asked the doctor the questions she'd been swallowing for a month. So." He set the bag on the counter. "He liked these cut into stars."

Jackson carried the mangoes to the break room, took out the little paring knife, and began cutting.

activity: to write a database query that joins two tables to find which customers ordered nothing
story:
The assignment on the board read "Customers who ordered nothing," and Tyler read it four times before it stopped looking like a contradiction. Mr. Okafor had given them two tables, Customers and Orders, and a question that seemed to assume you could search for something that wasn't there. Tyler opened his laptop next to Priya, who was already typing, and behind them Marcus was holding forth as he always did, this time about how anyone who spelled out the letters S, Q, L was basically admitting they'd never touched a real database.

"It's sequel," Marcus said, leaning his chair back onto two legs. "Nobody who actually works says it letter by letter."

"My cousin works at a bank," Priya said without looking up, "and she says S-Q-L, every day, and nobody has fired her yet."

"You're being doctrinaire about it," Tyler said, mostly to get Marcus to stop rocking, and Marcus looked wounded in the theatrical way that meant he'd keep the argument going all period. Tyler turned back to his screen. He typed the join he understood, Customers joined to Orders on customer ID, ran it, and got a tidy list of exactly the people who had bought something. The question wanted the opposite. He tried adding NOT to the condition and got a wall of duplicates so long the scroll bar shrank to a sliver.

"Your INNER JOIN subsumes them," Priya said, glancing over. "Every customer with one order gets swallowed into the match, so the no-order people never show up at all." She tapped his screen. "You need the join that keeps the left side even when the right side is empty."

"A LEFT JOIN," Tyler said, and she shrugged, unimpressed by his parroting, which was fair. He retyped it, Customers LEFT JOIN Orders, ran it, and there they were, every customer, with blank spaces where the order columns should be for a handful of names. Not nothing, exactly. Empty cells. He stared at the nulls, the little gaps that meant nobody had ever clicked buy, and it occurred to him that the trick wasn't finding nothing, it was making nothing visible so you could filter for it. He added WHERE Orders.order_id IS NULL, and the list shrank to eleven names. Mrs. Adeyemi. R. Cortez. A person called Test Account 3.

"It's pronounced sequel," Marcus announced from behind them, "because that's literally what it was called. Look." He turned his laptop around to show a scanned page from some ancient IBM document, yellow-edged, the typeface like a typewriter's. Tyler leaned over and read it aloud, quietly, so the rest of the lab wouldn't hear: SQL was developed at IBM in the early 1970s by Donald Chamberlin and Raymond Boyce, and was first called SEQUEL.

"So we're both right," Priya said, which Marcus received like a hostage negotiation. "The old-timers say sequel because of the original name, and everyone else spells it out."

"That's not both right, that's me being more historically authentic."

"It's metonymy," Priya said. Marcus blinked. "Calling the whole language by one old name, like calling your car your wheels. It doesn't make you authentic, it makes you a poetic device." Tyler laughed into his sleeve, and Priya allowed herself half a smile before going back to her code.

Tyler looked at his eleven names again. Somewhere in the fact Marcus had dug up, in a language renamed but still doing the same work fifty years later, there was something that matched his query: the thing that persists, showing up in every result, even though its original label had gone empty. He decided not to say that out loud, because Marcus would either steal it or mock it, and because he wasn't sure the comparison actually held. It might just be a coincidence of mood. He filed it under uncertain, which was a bigger folder than it used to be.

Mr. Okafor drifted by and looked at Tyler's screen, arms folded. "Eleven customers, Mr. Reyes. Can you tell me why the nulls were necessary?" Tyler started to explain the left side surviving the empty right, and Priya cut in, deadpan, "He learned it from a poet. We call the language SEQUEL now, for authenticity." Marcus raised both hands in triumph.

"Sequel," Mr. Okafor said mildly, and walked on.

story:
The kiln had been broken since March, so the community studio smelled of acrylic and turpentine instead of fired clay, and Sarah had claimed the table by the window because its light came in flat and honest across the afternoon. Her portfolio was due in nine days. On the table lay her third attempt at the harbor piece: gray water, gray sky, a line of pilings marching out toward a buoy that refused to matter.

"You've got the horizon dead center," said Priya, leaning over from the easel she shared with two oil painters who never came on Saturdays. "Put it a third of the way down. Rule of thirds."

Sarah sat back. "Who made that a rule?"

Priya shrugged, already turning back to her canvas. "Some dead guy, probably."

That should have been the end of it. Instead Sarah found herself that evening in the college library, because the studio kept a shelf of donated art books and the shelf had failed her, and there was something in the question that wouldn't quiet down. She wasn't the kind of person who introspect her way into libraries, or at least she hadn't been; apparently she was now. She found it in a scanned copy of an old book, its pages photographed so carefully she could see the foxing: Remarks on Rural Scenery, by John Thomas Smith, 1797. He had written the phrase down first, "rule of thirds," in a book about rural scenery, of all things, two hundred and odd years before Priya told her to move her horizon. She copied the citation onto the back of a gas receipt and rode the late bus home holding it like a ticket.

The next Saturday she arrived first and redrew the harbor. Horizon a third of the way down, the pilings entering from the left, the buoy now sitting, not floating, at a point that felt almost unfairly deliberate. The painting looked better. That was the trouble with it. It looked like every photograph on every wall of every dentist's office she had ever sat in, a composition so absorbed into the world that using it felt like quoting without speech marks.

"See?" Priya said when she came in, coat still on, shaking rain off it. "Told you."

"It's from a book," Sarah said. "John Thomas Smith, 1797. Remarks on Rural Scenery. First wrote down the phrase 'rule of thirds.'"

"Okay," said Priya, delighted and uninterested at once, the way she was about most things that weren't paint. "So it's old. Old things work."

But Sarah had spent the week thinking about how a man looking at rural scenery in 1797 had casually set a boundary she was now standing inside, and how her grandmother's quilts ignored every such law and still stopped your breath, and how the pilings in the actual harbor at Revere Beach did not arrange themselves in thirds. The rain intensified against the window, streaking the light she had chosen the table for. She picked up a rag and wiped the buoy off. Then she wiped the horizon off, the whole careful line of it, and let the gray water and the gray sky bleed into each other at a height chosen by nothing but her own wrist.

Priya watched this with genuine alarm. "You're going to submit that?"

"I don't know what I'm going to submit," Sarah said, which was true, and which cost her something to say out loud, because the portfolio wanted confidence and she had been practicing confidence all autumn like a scale.

The afternoon organized itself around her not deciding. A retired man named Walter, loquacious after his second thermos of coffee, narrated his own progress on a lighthouse to anyone in range. Two kids from the high school argued about whether orange was a real color. Priya painted in her deliberate, stabbing way and did not mention the horizon again, though Sarah caught her looking, twice, at the place where water met nothing.

Near closing, Sarah did a small thing. In the lower third of the canvas, roughly, though she refused to measure, she set the buoy back in, small and black against the formless gray. Not at an intersection, not at a power point, whatever those were called. Just low and left of center, where a buoy would actually ride. The rest she left unresolved, water and sky agreeing to be the same color, the pilings dissolving at their tops like an archipelago seen through fog, half-real.

"That's it?" Priya said, packing her brushes.

"That's what I have," Sarah said.

Priya stood in front of it for longer than she stood in front of anything, head tilted, and Sarah understood that the verdict, whatever it was, would not be spoken tonight. Walter shut off the lights from the switch by the door, and the harbor went dark all at once, water, sky, and buoy together.

activity: to compute the electric field strength at a point between two charged plates
story:
The gymnasium smelled of floor wax and hot extension cords, and Maxime had been adjusting the gap between his two aluminum plates for an hour before the judges started circulating. His project was a field-mapping rig: a pair of plates on a micrometer stand, a small probe, a hand-drawn graph of field strength versus position. The numbers had come out cleanly last night, which was the problem, because they had come out too cleanly, and he had not slept well thinking about it.

Noor set up beside him at eight with her terrariums and a folder of bee diagrams. She wanted, she had told him twice on the bus, an interview with the local paper, because the paper only ever photographed the robotics team and she was tired of bees being subsumed under the general heading of science-fair variety acts. She straightened her label cards and glanced at his rig. "Still cooking, Volta?"

"Verifying." He uncapped his marker and redid the arithmetic on the back of his data sheet, slowly, the way his father balanced a checkbook. He had twelve hundred volts across a gap of half a millimetre. Divide the one by the other and the field between his plates came out at over two billion volts per metre. He wrote it, looked at it, and crossed it out with a single line.

"That's a big number," Noor said, reading over his shoulder.

"It's a broken number." He tapped the power supply, a gray brick of uncertain provenance that he had bought secondhand from a man at a flea market who had assured him it worked. "If the field were really that strong, the air between the plates wouldn't just sit there."

She frowned at the gap, so narrow he could slip a playing card through it and feel the drag. "What would it do?"

"It would spark. Dry air breaks down around three million volts per metre, sea-level pressure. So there's a limit, an actual ceiling on how strong a field can be across an air gap." He said it and then heard it, and something in his chest went quiet. His whole graph was impossible. Every point on it was a field the air itself would not permit.

The first judge arrived before he could panic properly. She was a woman with reading glasses on a chain, and she bent close to his graph, then closer to the plates. "Walk me through your field calculation."

"Twelve hundred volts, half a millimetre, so I divide." He turned the sheet toward her. "Except the answer's wrong, because the air would have sparked long before I got there, and it didn't spark. I've been running it for an hour."

The judge said nothing, which was somehow worse than a question. Noor leaned in and tapped the micrometer stand itself. "Maxime. Look at your spacers."

He looked. He had built the stand from brass shim stock, and the spacers, the little strips that set the plate separation, were stamped with their thickness. He had assumed half a millimetre because the packet had said so at the flea market, from the same man, with the same assurance. The stamp on the actual strips in the actual stand read 0.5 mm. He measured them anyway with the school's calipers, borrowing them from the physics storeroom through a door Ms. Achterberg left unlocked for him. The strips measured 0.4 millimetres, and worse, they were not matched; one was thicker than the other by a tenth, so his plates had been tilted all morning, and his field had never been uniform at all.

The judge was watching him measure. "So where does that leave your data?"

"Equivocal," Maxime said. "That's the honest word for it. The field between the plates was never what I computed, because the gap was never what I assumed, and even if it had been, the air caps the whole thing at three million volts per metre anyway. If my numbers had been right, I'd have gotten a spark, not a graph." He heard himself say it and realized it was the first sentence of the entire project that he fully believed.

The judge wrote something short in her book, thanked him, and moved on to Noor's terrariums, where she stayed for ten minutes and asked about waggle dances. Noor answered steadily, eyes bright. When the woman finally left, Noor exhaled and squeezed Maxime's arm. "That was a real judge question and you gave a real answer. That's better than a pretty graph."

Maxime pulled his graph down off the board and turned the paper over to its blank side. He drew a new axis, wrote "measured, not assumed" at the top, and began remeasuring the gap with the calipers, plate by plate, recording each number as it came. Somewhere behind him a buzzer sounded for the second round of judging, and a boy two tables over yelped as his homemade Tesla coil threw a spark across six centimetres of open air.

"See," Noor said, not looking up from her bees. "Even the air has rules."

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
story:
The restaurant had pushed four tables together under the big screen, and by the second quarter Sarah's uncle Theo had already lost a trivia bet to her cousin Marcus twice, which meant he owed him twenty dollars and a plate of nachos he kept trying to amortize by eating himself. Sarah sat between her grandmother and her best friend Priya, nominally watching the game, actually watching Marcus. He was the one who had told her, at the graduation party last month, that she argued like a lawyer and cared about nothing, and she had been carrying that sentence around ever since like a stone in her shoe.

"There's a trivia contest at halftime," Marcus announced, waving the paper flyer the waitress had left. "Winner gets fifty bucks off the bill. Sports and Olympics stuff, since the games start next month."

"I'll do it," Sarah said, before she could think better of it.

"You don't watch sports," her grandmother said, not unkindly.

"I watch the Olympics. I like the opening ceremony. All the flags."

"Lugubrious music, everyone crying," Priya agreed, tearing a piece of napkin into small flags of her own. "It's the best thing on television."

The first half was a grinding, low-scoring affair that Uncle Theo narrated like a funeral oration, and by halftime Sarah had two of the three trivia questions right, tied with a man in a trucker hat from the bar who turned out to know an alarming amount about boxing. Then the waitress cleared her throat and read the tiebreaker: which colors appear in the five Olympic rings, and why those colors.

Sarah closed her eyes. The rings were blue, yellow, black, green, and red, she was sure of that. But the why escaped her, and she could feel Marcus across the table, grinning, waiting for her to fail so he could add it to his collection of evidence that she was all talk. She thought about the opening ceremonies she had actually watched, the part she liked best, the parade where every country came in behind its flag. She had once spent a whole afternoon as a kid hunting for her own country's colors in the rings on a poster in her grandfather's study, tracing them with her finger, and her grandfather had told her the answer then, and she had forgotten it, and now it came back the way forgotten things do, all at once and slightly sideways.

"They picked the colors so every national flag at the time had at least one of them," she said, opening her eyes. "That includes the white background of the rings." She paused. "And it was Pierre de Coubertin who designed them. Nineteen thirteen."

The waitress looked at her card. "That's... that's it exactly. Wow. Okay."

The trucker hat man raised his glass to her from the bar, which felt almost better than the fifty dollars. Almost, because the fifty dollars was real, and when Uncle Theo launched into a peroration about how they should put it toward his nachos debt to Marcus, Sarah held the flyer above her head out of his reach and said the money was going to dessert, split eight ways, and that his debts were his own affair.

"You knew that off the top of your head," Marcus said as the second half started and everyone leaned back toward the screen. "Sports trivia."

"It's not sports trivia. It's flags. There's a difference."

"There's really not."

"You said I care about nothing," Sarah said, keeping her voice light, because they were in public and because she was not sure she wanted the answer anyway. "I care about a French guy in 1913 who wanted every country to see itself in one symbol. That's something."

Marcus considered this while the crowd on screen and the crowd in the restaurant roared at a fumble. "So you're saying you care about, what, symbolism."

"I'm saying I care about the specific argument that you can make something universal without erasing anybody. He didn't pick colors for his country. He picked colors so nobody's country would be left out." She heard herself and laughed a little. "Which might be generous or might just be good design, I honestly can't tell, and I'm not sure it matters which."

"That's the most Sarah sentence ever spoken," Priya said, and stole the last tortilla chip.

The game tightened in the fourth quarter, and the restaurant rose and fell with it, and Sarah found she was standing too, shouting at the screen with her grandmother's hand gripping her arm. She still couldn't have named more than three players. She was still watching. On the wall above the screen somebody had taped up a paper promotion for the Olympics next month, five rings printed small in the corner, and every time the crowd noise dipped she found her eyes drifting to it, white showing between the colors.

With eleven seconds left and the score tied, Marcus leaned over and said, "Double or nothing on dessert. Field goal is good."

"Done," Sarah said, and did not look away from the ball.
