activity: going on a first date
story:
Victor had told Theo he was an excellent skater, which was true in the sense that he had once, in seventh grade, completed a full lap without touching the wall. The rink's fluorescent glare found him out within eleven seconds, when his feet performed a decision of their own and deposited him against the boards with a sound like a filing cabinet falling downstairs.

"You said intermediate," Priya said, gliding backward in front of him, hands in her coat pockets, entirely at ease on the ice in a way that seemed almost personal, as though the rink had taken her side.

"Intermediate is a spectrum," Victor said from the floor. "I'm on it."

"Where on it?"

"The floor part of it." He got up, and she laughed, and the laugh did something to his chest that he chose not to examine in front of witnesses.

She had asked him out, actually, which he kept forgetting to be honest with himself about. In his own telling, the whole thing had been his maneuver: the note in AP Gov about her locker sticker for a band he liked, the three days of strategic hovering. The truth, which he set aside the way one sets aside a bill, was that she had turned around in class and said, "You're the one who owns the same shirt as me in a worse color, we should skate sometime," and he had said "Obviously," and then gone into the hallway and stared at a fire extinguisher for a while.

They did laps, halting and smooth respectively. She coached him through crossovers; he expostulated that the wall was closer than it looked, and the wall, his true nemesis on the ice, proved his point by catching his elbow. At the snack bar they split a pretzel the size of a steering wheel and argued about whether the Zamboni driver had a favorite, the way teachers had favorites. "He resurfaces a lane of honor," Priya said. "For people he respects. You'll never see it." Victor said that was virulent propaganda against a man who drove a machine that was basically a giant iron, and she laughed again, and he began to hope the evening was something they would both want to remember in the same direction.

He was careful all night, and proud of the carefulness. He asked before taking her hand on the ice, and when they stood in the parking lot afterward, cold coming up through their shoes, he asked before anything else too, and she said yes, and kissed him briefly, and he floated approximately four inches off the asphalt.

Then, walking toward her car, she slowed. "Okay, so," she said. "I think I'd rather just say goodnight here. I'm kind of done with being touched tonight. Not a verdict on you."

His first impulse was to debate it, and he saw himself doing so, some version of him already opening his mouth to point out that she had kissed him, that the yes had happened, that in the court of Victor's feelings the evidence was overwhelming. He shut that version up. Somewhere in the fog of his own confidence, a fact surfaced from a health assembly he'd half ignored: consent to any intimate contact could be withdrawn at any time, even after it was first given. Yes was not a contract. Yes was a weather report, good until it wasn't.

"That's completely fine," he said, and meant it, mostly, and the part of him that didn't was a part he could admit existed without letting it drive.

"You paused," she said, watching him. "That was a good pause. I've seen worse pauses. Some guys treat a kiss like a lease."

"A lease can't be revoked," Victor said. "Consent can. Any time, even after it was given. Which I definitely knew before tonight and did not just assemble from first principles in your parking lot."

"Smooth," she said. "Devastatingly smooth." She unlocked her car, then turned back, keys jingling against her palm. "Same time next week? You can fall down for me again."

"I'll bring a helmet," Victor said. "For the boards. They've been asking for a rematch."

She grinned and got in, and he stood in the cold until her taillights turned out of the lot, then skated the walk home on the frozen patches of sidewalk, badly, gloriously, without falling once.

activity: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
story:
The elevator in the Blakely Arms smelled like wet cardboard and broke somewhere between the third and fourth floor every other day, so Audrey took the stairs, counting them out of habit, the way she used to count the steps to Marisol's porch. The movers had left her boxes in the living room in a tower that leaned slightly, and her mother was already at the new job, so it was Audrey alone who carried her desk lamp up six flights and set it on the windowsill facing the airshaft. From that window she could see a strip of the school three blocks off, the flagpole, the flat roof of the gymnasium. At the old house the window had faced Marisol's window, and they had signaled each other with flashlight beams after their mothers declared lights-out, one flash for hello, two for come outside.

School started on a Tuesday. In homeroom the teacher, a narrow man named Mr. Kestler whom the other students called a pedagogue in a tone that was not entirely affectionate, assigned Audrey a seat beside a girl named Priya Raghunathan. Priya lent her a pen without being asked and told her which stairwell avoided the crowd, and Audrey decided by Wednesday that Priya was the kind of person she would have been friends with already in the old town, which was a thought she kept to herself because it felt like a betrayal of somebody, though she could not have said of whom.

At night the apartment made noises the old house had not made. Pipes ticked, and a neighbor's television rose through the floor in muffled syllables. Audrey lay awake and found herself conducting an inventory she was ashamed of: the burr of her father's voice through the dining room wall, the lemon smell of Mrs. Ferreira's cleaning fluid on the shared stairwell, the particular slant of afternoon light across the biology lab where she and Marisol had dissected a fetal pig and laughed until Ms. Danner separated their stations. She was sixteen and in an apartment forty minutes from everything, and she missed a cleaning fluid. She resolved not to say this to anyone.

In the second week, in the cafeteria, Priya pushed her tray across from Audrey's without asking and sat down. Audrey had been looking at her phone, at a photograph Marisol had sent of the homecoming banner going up in the gymnasium, and she shut the screen off quickly, but Priya had seen it. "That's your old school," Priya said. It was not a question.

"My friend Marisol. They're decorating for homecoming." Audrey folded her napkin into smaller and smaller squares. "It's stupid. I've been here two weeks and I keep wanting to be back there, and it's only forty minutes. People commute farther than that for fun."

"Nobody talks about it here," Priya said, "but I looked it up when we moved, my sister's first year at college. The research on homesickness says nearly everyone who's away from home misses something about it. Almost everybody. Not just the weird kids. And it said around twenty percent of university students rate theirs at or above the midpoint of some severity scale." She stabbed a piece of broccoli. "So a fifth of them have it bad, and the rest still have it some. I found that out the week we moved here, and it made me feel less like a failure."

Audrey turned this over. She had been thinking of homesickness as a private defect, something to be subsumed under the general project of Starting Over, the way her mother had put it, new town, new chapter, as though the missing could be filed into a folder and the folder closed. If nearly everyone missed something, then the missing was not a failure of adaptation. It was closer to a tax everyone paid. But the severity scale bothered her, because twenty percent meant four out of five rated theirs below the midpoint, and Audrey had no idea where she fell on such a scale, and she suspected she fell higher than she wanted to admit.

That night she called Marisol. The connection was thin, and Marisol was halfway through a story about Danny Okafor and the banner committee, and Audrey listened and laughed in the right places, and when the story ended there was a pause in which the old signal system would have been useful, one flash for hello, two for come outside. "I miss it," Audrey said finally. "I miss you." Marisol said, "Obviously, you dork, it's been two weeks," and told her about the float, and the conversation moved on, and Audrey lay awake afterward and understood something she could not yet put in words: that missing was not the same as wanting to return, and that both were real, and that the two did not cancel out. She could be glad the apartment had a doorknob lock her mother let her use, and glad Priya existed, and still lie awake inventorying lemon smells. She did not know whether that was resilience or just confusion. She was honest with herself about not knowing.

The next Saturday the building had a tag sale in the courtyard, folding tables carried down by residents of all six floors. Audrey's mother contributed a lamp, a penurious contribution to the communal effort that the woman from 4C noted aloud with a short laugh, though the lamp sold within the hour for four dollars. Priya appeared with her younger brother and forty minutes of the afternoon to spend, and they walked the tables, and Audrey bought a chipped ceramic bowl with a blue rim for fifty cents because it was the exact blue of the old kitchen.

They took the bowl up the six flights, stopping on the third-floor landing where the afternoon light came through the stairwell window at a slant, and stood there a moment, both of them looking at it. "My sister says it gets quieter in your head after a month or two," Priya said. "Not gone. Just quieter."

"That's fine," Audrey said. "I don't need it gone."

She set the bowl on the windowsill beside the lamp, where it would catch whatever light the airshaft allowed, and went back down for the last box.

The pump at the community garden broke on the first Saturday of June, and by noon the okra leaves had gone soft at the edges, folding like hands. Jonathan had been coming since April to earn the last service hours his school required, but he kept coming after the hours ran out, and he could not have said exactly why. Maybe because Ms. Reyes, who ran the garden, had once let him take home a tomato still warm from the fence line, and the taste of it had enthralled him in a way that no grocery-store tomato ever had, a sweetness with something almost bitter underneath.

Now he stood at the pump with Ravi, a community college student who interned there on Saturdays, while the two of them listened to the motor grind and deliver nothing. "The city raised the water rate in March," Ravi said. "Half the gardens on this side of town turned their plots to gravel. Ms. Reyes is paying out of her own pocket." He wiped his hands on his jeans. "There's a meeting Thursday about a new hookup. Somebody's offering free water."

"Free water doesn't exist," Jonathan said, because his father said that about nothing being free, and his father was usually right in ways that took years to see.

The meeting was held under the tin-roofed pavilion, and it was there that Jonathan learned where the free water came from. A man in a golf shirt explained that a bottling company two blocks north was offering runoff from its filtration system, enough to fill the tanks twice a week, in exchange for a small thing: the garden would sign a letter supporting the company's permit application to take more water from the aquifer. "It's a win-win," the man said. "You get water. They get goodwill."

Ms. Reyes said nothing, which Jonathan had learned was her way of saying a great deal. An older man named Fitz, who grew collards on the corner plot, said the aquifer was already dropping; his well at home had gone sour with sulfur the summer before. The man in the golf shirt smiled and said the aquifer was a big system, complicated, and that one permit would hardly matter.

That night Jonathan typed "aquifer depletion" into his laptop and followed a thread he had not expected. It led him to the Aral Sea. He read the sentence three times: the Soviet Union had diverted the Amu Darya and the Syr Darya rivers to irrigate cotton, and the shrinking, saltier Aral Sea had lost a fishing industry that had once employed about 40,000 people. Rivers sent elsewhere to grow one thing; a sea dying downstream; forty thousand people whose work simply evaporated. He thought about the bottling plant two blocks north, and the gardens south of it, and Fitz's sulfur well, and he understood that he was not reading history. He was reading a template.

The next Saturday, a group of tenth graders arrived for a field lesson, part of some school partnership, and Ravi put Jonathan in charge of the irrigation demo while he fixed the pump line. Jonathan showed them the drip tape, the timers, the rain barrels. Then a girl named Priya asked why the garden couldn't just take the free water, and Jonathan told them about the Aral Sea. "Somebody upstream got water for cotton," he said, "and the people downstream lost the sea." He pointed at the tanks. "The plant is upstream. We're downstream, until somebody else is downstream of us."

"Is that like a rule?" Priya asked.

"It's more like a heuristic," Jonathan said. "A shortcut for thinking. When somebody offers you water, ask who ends up with less."

Priya nodded slowly, and then she said the thing that turned the whole afternoon sideways. "My dad works at the plant," she said. "If they don't get the permit, he gets laid off in the fall. He told my mom last week." She looked at the okra, at the drip tape, at her shoes. "Forty thousand people somewhere. My dad here."

Jonathan had been building an argument all week, and now it stood in front of him in a polo shirt with a father. He thought of a day years ago, before the garden existed, when he and his own father had walked past this same corner and his father had called it a wasteland, and Jonathan, ten years old, had found a milkweed growing through the chain-link and had carried the seed pod home in his fist. Even then something in him had believed that a place could change. Now he was less sure whether belief was a heuristic too, and whether heuristics were honest or just comforting.

He thought about it the way his economics teacher had taught him to hold two ideas at once: the garden needed water to live; the plant's workers needed the permit to live; both of those things could be true, and the permit could still take water from someone further down the line whom no one at the meeting would ever meet. He could oppose the letter and feel clean, or support it and feel useful, and neither position covered the whole cost.

Thursday evening, at the second meeting, Ms. Reyes called for a vote. The pavilion was full, Fitz on one side and the man in the golf shirt on the other, and Priya's father stood quietly by the ice chest, a man with calluses Jonathan recognized because his own father had them too. Ms. Reyes looked around the circle and said, "Jonathan, you've been here every week. What do you think?"

Jonathan stood up. Outside, the drip tape he had repaired that morning was releasing its slow bright beads onto the okra, each one catching the last of the light before it disappeared into the dirt.

story:
Layla arrived early enough to claim a folding chair in the second row of the community center, with her notebook open and a petition of two hundred and twelve signatures paper-clipped to the inside cover. The petition asked the town to install a pedestrian signal at the crossing on Route 9, where her brother Aiden had been clipped by a pickup in October and had walked with a cane since. The town council had put the crossing ordinance on tonight's agenda, and the agenda's dry phrasing, "First reading; discussion; possible vote," adumbrated everything that mattered to her without promising any of it.

The meeting opened with the clerk reading the ordinance aloud, word for word, the way a draftsman had written it: "Section 1. The Department of Public Works shall install a illuminated pedestrian signal." A councilwoman named Ortiz interrupted to say that it should be "an illuminated," and the clerk penciled the correction in, and Layla wrote in her notebook that even a comma of the law had to be argued over before it could exist. The town attorney had reviewed the draft for conflicts with state statutes, and the public safety committee had met twice and signed off, and all of this had happened invisibly over three months while Layla called the clerk's office every Friday to ask whether anything had moved.

Then came the debate. A saturnine councilman named Braddock, who owned the hardware store and spoke slowly as though every word cost him inventory, said the town's budget could not absorb forty thousand dollars for a signal that would serve, in his estimate, a dozen schoolchildren a day. "There is a crosswalk painted there already," he said. "Paint is not nothing." Layla's hand went up before she had fully decided to raise it.

She stood at the microphone with her knees shaking and read from her notes. She described Aiden's route to school, the forty-mile-per-hour traffic, the two hundred and twelve names. She said that paint was not nothing, she would grant that, but that paint assumed drivers would look, and the driver who hit Aiden had been looking at his phone. She said she had counted the children herself, on four separate mornings, and the number was twenty-three, not twelve. When she sat down, an old man behind her leaned forward and said, "Good girl," and she could not decide whether to be pleased or embarrassed, so she was both.

The council debated for another twenty minutes, Ortiz arguing that the county might cover half the cost, Braddock conceding that point reluctantly, and then the mayor called the roll. Five voted yes, one voted no, Braddock, and the ordinance passed on its first reading, which the clerk noted would be followed by a second reading and then, upon final passage, the mayor's signature. Layla wrote down the sequence, drafting, review, debate, votes, signature, and beside it she wrote: it worked. Then, because she was honest with herself even in notebooks, she added: here, anyway.

During the public comment period that followed, a man she recognized as Mr. Pham, who taught civics at the high school but who was here tonight as a private citizen wearing a lawn-mowing shirt, stood up to ask a question of the state senator who had driven out to attend. The senator's bill, which would fund safety upgrades at dangerous crossings statewide through a matching grant program, was the reason Layla's forty thousand dollars might shrink to twenty. Mr. Pham asked why, when the papers said fifty-five senators supported it, it had still failed. "Fifty-five is a majority," he said. "What am I missing?"

The senator rubbed his eyes. "Ending most debate in the Senate takes cloture," he said. "Since 1975, cloture has required three-fifths of the senators. With all hundred seats filled, that's sixty votes." He let that sit for a moment. "So fifty-five supporters can want a bill very much and still not get to vote on it."

Layla sat with that. In her notebook she wrote 60, then circled it, then drew a line from it back to the roll call she had just witnessed, where five votes out of seven had been enough because seven was the whole universe of that decision. She had come tonight with a simple theory of change, the theory of her petition: gather enough voices and the right thing happens. The theory had worked two rows from where she sat. The same theory, scaled up, had died in a building she had never entered, not because the voices were too few to be a majority but because the rules asked for more than a majority, and she did not yet know whether that rule protected small towns like hers from being steamrolled or simply protected whoever was already standing still.

While the senator fielded another question, her phone buzzed. A text from Priya, who was at home studying for the AP Biology exam: "how was town hall?? also please explain speciation to me at lunch, i keep confusing it with evolution generally. isolated populations drift apart until they can't come back together even if you put them side by side." Layla read it twice. She typed, "meeting was good, tell you tomorrow," and then, before she could talk herself out of it, "is speciation ever reversible?" Priya's answer came as three thinking dots that vanished without becoming anything.

After the meeting broke up, people milled around the coffee urn, and Layla found herself beside the senator, who was folding his own agenda into quarters. She asked him whether the crossing bill was dead for good. "Bills don't die the way people think," he said. "They get folded into other bills, or they wait for a different Senate, or a different year." He looked at her notebook, still open in her hands. "You taking notes for a class?"

"For my brother," Layla said, and showed him the page with the circled 60.

He nodded slowly, the way Braddock had spoken, as if it cost him something. "Keep both numbers," he said. "Five out of seven, and sixty out of a hundred. They're both true at the same time, and someday you'll have to decide which one you're willing to live inside."

She walked home past the crossing on Route 9, where the painted stripes were faded to a ghost of themselves in her headlights-shadowed view, and stood for a moment at the edge of the road, waiting for a gap in the traffic.

The skate park was mostly empty by five, the September light going long and gold across the concrete bowls, and Charlotte had the picnic table by the fence to herself, which was the only reason she'd brought her physics homework here at all. Her brother Theo had cajoled her into coming with the promise of a ride and the threat of telling their mother she was failing, and she had brought the textbook as a kind of shield, something to hold between herself and the afternoon. Now he was somewhere below in the shallow bowl, dropping in again and again, and she was stuck on a problem about a charged ball launched between two metal plates, one with an angle and a speed and no obvious mercy.

She understood the launch part better than she'd expected to. You took the velocity and split it, horizontal piece and vertical piece, and then the two directions went their separate ways, one coasting steadily like a stone skipped across still water, the other rising and falling under gravity's ledger. She'd gotten that far at the kitchen table last night, drawing little arrows until her pen ran dry. What she couldn't figure out was the plates. The problem said the ball was launched somewhere between two large parallel plates, and it asked for the force on it, and Charlotte had spent twenty minutes with her ruler trying to work out how far the ball was from each plate, because surely that distance mattered, surely a point close to one plate felt something different from a point in the middle. She'd measured the diagram so many times the numbers had gone soft in her head.

A boy about her age coasted up to the table to retrieve his water bottle, which someone had set on the far end, and paused when he saw the page. "Physics," he said. "I did that unit last year. You look like you're about to burn the book."

"I'm trying to find where the ball is between the plates," Charlotte said. "Like how close to each one."

He tipped his head, considering, in no hurry to leave. "Between big parallel plates it's basically the same everywhere in the middle," he said. "Away from the edges, a point near one plate has the same field strength as a point halfway between them. My teacher made us test it and then told us we'd wasted a class proving we could have skipped it." He shrugged, grabbed his bottle, and rolled off toward the bowl, leaving her staring at a diagram she'd covered in pencil measurements that meant nothing.

She erased them slowly, all the little tick marks, and the erasure felt like both a loss and a door swinging open. All that arithmetic, discarded. But if position didn't matter, then the field was just the field, uniform as a held breath, and the force came out in two lines instead of twenty. She checked her result twice because a thing that easy seemed like it must be hiding something, and the second check agreed with the first, and she wrote her answer small, as if to apologize for its size.

"Who's the nerd whisperer?" Theo asked, climbing the fence a few minutes later, hair stuck to his forehead. He nodded at the departing boy, who was now attempting something on the coping of the bowl with a small crowd of younger skaters watching him like acolytes.

"He told me the answer to my homework," Charlotte said. "More or less."

"That's cheating."

"It's not cheating. He told me what kind of problem it is. I still had to do it." She turned the notebook toward Theo, who looked at it with the polite blankness he saved for her schoolwork, and then, because he was her brother and knew her too well, said, "You're going to spend all night checking whether he was right, aren't you."

"Probably," she admitted. That was the part she couldn't explain to him, that trusting a stranger's sentence felt different from trusting her own pencil, and that tomorrow she would go to the physics room before first bell and find out one way or the other, and either way the certainty she had right now was borrowed, equivocal, a coin she hadn't bitten yet. She looked at her answer again. It sat there in her small handwriting, plausible and unproven.

The younger skaters had gone quiet because the boy was dropping in from the highest edge now, and Charlotte watched him go down the curve and up the far side, the board leaving his feet for half a second, and she thought, without meaning to, that he was all one velocity at the top of the arc, his horizontal and vertical selves crossed at a single instant before gravity started its collecting. He landed it. The little crowd thumped their boards against the concrete, that hollow applause skate parks make instead of clapping.

"Again," one of the small kids said, and the boy climbed the ramp to try it a second time, because once was luck and twice was knowing, and Charlotte closed her notebook on her two-line answer and slid off the bench to watch.

story:
Gavin had the garage to himself until six, which gave him three hours to make the launcher do something other than hum accusingly at him. The machine sat on the workbench between a coffee can of bolts and his father's putative lawn mower, the one that had never once cut grass but had somehow earned permanent bench space. He fed a tennis ball into the wheel assembly, set the barrel to thirty degrees, and pressed the switch. The ball sailed over the driveway, bounced off the recycling bin, and rolled into the hedge.

"Sixteen feet," said Priya, who was crouched at the edge of the driveway with a tape measure and her chin on her fist. "Maybe seventeen. The fair is Saturday, Gavin. Marcus's team has a pneumatic cannon."

"Marcus's team also has matching T-shirts. They've lost the plot." He walked the ball back, reset the angle to sixty degrees, and fired again. This time the ball climbed steeply, hung at its apex like a reluctant thought, and dropped barely eight feet from the bench. Priya wrote the number without comment, which was worse than laughing.

Gavin sat down on the mower and stared at his physics notebook, open to the page he'd copied off the board without understanding. Horizontal and vertical velocity, the teacher had said, are independent of each other, so you treat them separately. At the time it had sounded like a rule for filing paperwork. Now he looked at his two data points and felt the first loose tooth of an idea. High angle, short distance. Low angle, also short. Somewhere between, the ball had to travel farther than either.

"Try forty-five," Priya said.

"That's suspiciously specific."

"Mr. Okafor said it in class. Something about forty-five degrees." She flipped back through her own notes, found the margin where she'd scrawled it during a lecture she'd mostly spent drawing a duck. "Yeah. He said on level ground with no air resistance, forty-five degrees gives the greatest range for a given launch speed."

"We have air resistance."

"We have a tennis ball and a dream. Try it."

Gavin adjusted the barrel, checked it twice against the protractor taped to the hinge, and fired. The ball left the wheels in a clean, low arc, struck the driveway past the recycling bin, past the hedge, and rolled to a stop against the curb at the property line. Priya measured twice because she didn't believe the first number. Thirty-one feet.

"It's the splitting thing," Gavin said, pacing now, notebook in hand. "The launch speed gets divided between going up and going forward. Steeper, and more of it goes up, so the ball spends forever in the air but never gets anywhere. Flatter, and it crosses out fast but barely hangs at all." He drew two arrows off a single slanted line, one horizontal, one vertical, and for the first time all semester the arrows looked like something real, like the shadow and the height of the same ball at the same moment. Forty-five split the speed evenly enough that neither half incapacitated the other, and the ball stayed airborne long enough to use all its forward push.

Priya fired while Gavin marked angles in five-degree increments, then two, then one. Forty-three gave thirty feet. Forty-six gave thirty. Forty-five, three trials running, gave thirty-one, give or take the wobble in the wheels. When they tried a harder golf ball, the numbers stretched but the shape held: the peak of their little graph sat stubbornly at forty-five degrees, and everything Gavin knew said that on actual level ground with actual still air, that was where the maximum lived. He wrote the caveat in the corner of the graph anyway, because the driveway sloped two inches toward the curb and he couldn't prove it didn't matter.

His father came through the garage door at ten past six, saw the graph, and leaned over it with his reading glasses halfway down his nose. "Forty-five," he said. "Huh. My coach always told us to kick low."

"Your coach was no iconoclast," Priya said.

"My coach made us run laps for asking questions." His father tapped the paper. "So Saturday, you set it to forty-five and hope Marcus's T-shirts don't shoot farther?"

"We set it to forty-five and we know why," Gavin said. He picked up the golf ball, weighed it in his palm, and looked down the barrel at the darkening street beyond the open door. "Fire it once more before we lose the light."

story:
The paper came back on a Thursday, folded once, with a red note across the top that read "This is not a bibliography." Ryan read it four times on the walk to the café, as though repetition might change the words, and by the time he ordered his medium drip he had stopped being offended and started being curious, which he suspected was a bad sign about his personality.

He spread the pages across the small table by the window, the one that wobbled unless you shimmed it with a napkin. Eight pages on the Hollywood blacklist, for Mr. Harmon's history seminar. He had written it the only way he knew how, the way Ms. Ellery had drilled into them all last year: quotes followed by parentheses with a name and a number, and then, on its own page at the end, the full sources under the heading "Works Cited." Harmon wanted something else. The note at the bottom of the last page said footnotes, and the footnotes wanted a style called Chicago, and Chicago appeared to want everything about each source, in an order Ryan had never seen, with punctuation placed like landmines.

"You look like a man prognosticating," said Dana, setting down her own coffee across from him without asking. She had a battered LSAT prep book under her arm, its spine cracked in the middle the way spines crack when a person studies only on the days she feels like it. She wanted to argue, though. That was the thing about Dana. She would rather debate the blacklist for an hour than do a logic game, and Ryan sometimes suspected the law school plan existed mostly to give her a stage.

"Harmon says I don't have a bibliography," Ryan said. "I have Works Cited. Apparently that's a different animal."

"Is it?"

He turned to his English paper from October, which he'd brought because it was the only model he trusted. There, in Ellery's world, every borrowed sentence ended with a small parenthetical, the author's last name and a page number tucked into the parentheses, and the whole apparatus ran silently through the text like wiring in a wall. At the back, one page, plainly titled "Works Cited," each source written out in full. He'd never thought about the system as a system. It had simply been the temperature of the room.

"What's the difference?" Dana asked, stealing his muffin. He let her, because her want was larger than his want for the muffin, and because she would argue better with fuel.

"In Ellery's class, the citation is inside the paper." He tapped one of the parentheses, (Navasky 118), then a second, (Ceplair and Englund 204). "Name and page, right there where you use it. Then the full information lives at the end, on its own page, under that heading." He held up the October paper so she could see the words "Works Cited" centered at the top of the last page. "In Harmon's class, the information goes at the bottom of the page, in a footnote, and the whole list at the end is called a bibliography. I kept writing Works Cited where he wants the other word."

"So you wrote two papers and only one of them counts."

"Half of one counts." Ryan pulled the Chicago guide toward him, the library's copy, heavy as a paving stone, and found the page on footnotes. The number in the text was small and raised, and the note below carried the author's full name, the title, the facts of publication, all of it arranged with a formality that struck him as almost doctrinaire. He said so, and Dana said the law was worse, and for a moment they were both quiet out of respect for institutions older than they were.

He started converting. The first footnote took him eleven minutes and one text to a girl from class, who replied only with a shrug emoji. The second took four. By the fourth he could feel the logic of it, the way the raised numbers let the page keep talking while the evidence waited politely at the bottom, and he caught himself revising a sentence as he went, tightening a claim about the studios' testimony before Congress. He had written that the witnesses lied. That wasn't quite it. Lying implied shame, or at least concealment, and there was something worse in the transcripts, a mendacity so casual the men seemed bored by it. He typed the new sentence, then stopped.

"That's an argument," Dana said, reading over his shoulder. She had abandoned the logic games entirely, which Ryan noted and filed away for later use. "Before, you were just reporting. Now you're saying something someone could fight you about."

"That's the assignment, apparently. Harmon wrote 'Where do you stand?' on my draft, and I stood nowhere. I stood in a shrub."

"The shrub is very you." She drank her coffee and looked out the window at the parking lot, where someone was trying to parallel park a truck clearly designed for other purposes. "For the record, I think the parenthetical way is better. Cleaner. You don't have to keep dropping your eyes to the bottom of the page."

"Ellery would like you."

"Everyone likes me. It's a curse." But she had already pulled the prep book back toward herself, as if remembering she had her own paper due, in a sense, and Ryan went back to his footnotes, marking each raised number in pencil first, then ink, then checking each one against the guide like a man checking a lottery ticket twice.

The argument took shape around the fourth page, when he realized his two strongest sources disagreed with each other about whether the studio heads believed their own testimony, and that his whole case depended on which one he trusted, and that he could not fully decide. He left both in. He wrote a sentence saying the evidence cut both ways, footnoted it, and felt the small vertigo of admitting uncertainty in a document that was supposed to be an argument.

At the table by the window, the sun moved off the paper and onto Dana's prep book, and she closed it, and the truck in the lot finally slid into the space on the fifth attempt.

"Works Cited or bibliography?" she asked, nodding at his last page.

"Bibliography," Ryan said, and typed the word at the top of it, slowly, as though it might still change its mind.

story:
The monument stood where the school bus let them off, a granite shaft on a hillock of metamorphic rock hauled up in 1911 to honor the founders of Aldermoor, and Kaylee had chosen it for her college essay because she thought she already knew the story. The town's plaque said the first settlers had shared grain with the starving Mi'kmaq family wintering at the river bend, a moment of charity that supposedly gave the town its name. Her grandmother had said otherwise at Thanksgiving, spitting the words like pits: nobody shared anything, she said, they took the river and the fish weir and the winter camp, and the plaque was a story the founders told their grandchildren. Kayley wanted the truth before she wrote a word of it.

Her grandfather had come along because he liked the drive and because he was the only one left who had known any of the settlers' descendants. He walked the gravel path slowly, one hand on the shaft to steady himself, and listened while she read the plaque aloud. The wind came off the river smelling of mud and thaw.

"Your essay," he said. "You want to know if it happened."

"I want to know if I should write that it happened. There's a difference." She had been arguing this out for two weeks, first with the librarian, who had produced a folder of clippings all repeating the plaque, then with her grandmother, who had produced nothing but certainty. Between the two of them Kaylee felt like a musician trying to play two scores at once, and she was no virtuoso at this yet; she could only hold both pages open and hope.

The historical society kept its archive in the basement of the library, and that was where she had found the diary. Ezekiel Harrow, 1843, a founder's son, four years of weather and wheat prices and sermons. She had photographed every page. Now she sat on the monument's bottom step with the folder open on her knees, her grandfather beside her, and turned to the winter in question, the winter of the grain.

The pages for that December were full of oxen and a frozen well and the price of nails. There was no mention of a Mi'kmaq family at the river bend. No mention of grain given away. No mention of anyone starving at all.

"There," she said, and she heard her own triumph and didn't like the sound of it. "It never happened. He would have written it down. A whole family starving right there and he writes about nails."

Her grandfather was quiet for a moment. Then he laughed, a short bark that startled a crow off the monument's capstone. "An argument from silence," he said. "You can't do much with one of those."

"What do you mean, you can't do much with it?"

"Your grandmother used to try it on me. I'd forget our anniversary, and she'd say I clearly didn't love her because I never wrote her love letters." He was still smiling at the river. "But I never wrote anybody letters. I wrote grocery lists. She knew that."

Kaylee looked down at the pages of nails and oxen. "So because he didn't write it, doesn't mean it didn't happen."

"Doesn't mean it did, either." He tapped the folder with one finger. "He wrote what mattered to him. Whatever else went on, it wasn't the kind of thing he thought worth ink. Ask yourself why."

She sat with that, and the more she sat, the more the silence in the diary seemed to hold two shapes at once. If the grain had been given, it had been too ordinary to record, a small decency, not a founding. If the camp had been taken, that had been too ordinary too, the kind of taking that went without saying. Either way, the silence told her the founders hadn't thought the Mi'kmaq family remarkable, and that, she realized, was itself a kind of answer, though not the one either the plaque or her grandmother wanted. She tried to resuscitate the essay she had planned, the tidy one about charity confirmed or debunked, and couldn't. It lay there flat on the page.

"There's another diary," her grandfather said. "Half of one. Up at the house, in the seed drawer, of all places. Rebecca Harrow's. Never catalogued. Her great-granddaughter gave it to me when she cleared out the farm, and I keep meaning to take it to the society and never do." He looked at Kaylee, and something in his face was careful, the way he looked when he was deciding whether to hand over something breakable. "She was Ezekiel's sister. She wrote different things."

"You've read it?"

"Some." He looked back at the river. "Enough."

"Enough to know about the winter?"

They sat on the step together, the monument above them saying one thing in cut granite, the diary in her lap saying nothing in faded ink, and Kaylee understood suddenly that he had known, all along the drive and all the while on the path, exactly what was in Rebecca's half diary, and had brought her here first anyway. He wanted her to find it herself. Or he wanted her to be the kind of person who would notice what a silence could and couldn't prove before she went reading anyone's sister.

"Grandpa," she said. "Is it in the truck?"

He stood up, brushing gravel from his knees, and held out his hand for the folder, and she closed it and gave it to him, and they started down toward the parking lot, the river flashing between the bare trees.

"Rebecca kept a list," he said as he opened the passenger door for her. "Every family that came through, who they were, what they carried. She thought it mattered."
